sections.body: gofmt -l lists formatting differences without rewriting files. test checks packages; -race adds supported native race instrumentation. vet reports suspicious constructs rather than proving semantic correctness. A clean run still depends on meaningful tests.
sections.code:
gofmt -l .
go test ./...
go test -race ./...
go vet ./...
sections.walkthrough: Run each check and inspect its status. Race detection needs a supported native platform/toolchain and may require cgo; it is not available through every cross-compilation target. A race-free test run covers only paths actually exercised.

sections.title: Tidy deliberately and inspect the shipped binary
sections.body: mod tidy can add or remove module requirements and sums, so review its diff rather than running it as an invisible deployment step. build -trimpath removes local filesystem paths from the executable; version -m inspects embedded build/module metadata.
sections.code:
go mod tidy
git diff -- go.mod go.sum
mkdir -p bin
go build -trimpath -o ./bin/api ./cmd/api
go version -m ./bin/api
sections.walkthrough: The example assumes cmd/api exists. Test any module file changes before committing. Embedded build metadata is useful for provenance, but build flags and source state must still be recorded for reproducible releases.

takeaway: Check the selected module, format, test, race-check where supported, run vet and inspect the final artifact. Review dependency-file changes explicitly instead of treating tidy as a harmless read-only command.
reviewAnswer: Review the go.mod and go.sum changes before committing
question: What should you do after go mod tidy?
wrongAnswers: Assume it only prints dependency information
Delete go.sum because tidy makes it unnecessary
hint: Check the resulting dependency diff.
nuance: A race check covers executed paths and supported native targets, not every possible schedule.

title: HTTP debugging: curl, status codes and time budgets
objective: Probe a local API and separate DNS, connection, HTTP and application failures.
introduction: An API can fail before any handler runs, or return an HTTP error over a perfectly healthy connection. curl helps identify that boundary. These examples target your own local Go service at 127.0.0.1:8080 with a /healthz endpoint; adjust the paths to your application.

sections.title: Inspect headers and keep a timeout
sections.body: -i includes response headers, --connect-timeout bounds connection establishment, and --max-time bounds the total operation. --fail-with-body makes HTTP 4xx/5xx nonzero while retaining the response body, unlike an ordinary successful curl transport.
sections.code:
curl -i --connect-timeout 2 --max-time 5 \
  --fail-with-body http://127.0.0.1:8080/healthz
sections.walkthrough: Expect a successful health response from your server. Connection refused means no reachable listener at that address, not an HTTP 500. A timeout has a different cause again; retain the specific diagnostic instead of reducing all failures to unavailable.

sections.title: Send JSON without hiding the request contract
sections.body: --data-binary sends the provided bytes. The content type declares JSON, but the server still has to validate fields. This request is an example for a local /notes route accepting a text field; it is not an endpoint supplied by every Go service.
sections.code:
curl -i --max-time 5 --fail-with-body \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data-binary '{"text":"inspect this request"}' \
  http://127.0.0.1:8080/notes
sections.walkthrough: The single quotes keep Bash from interpreting the JSON double quotes. Data selects POST by default. Do not add a production authorization token to a shared example, shell history or a screenshot.

sections.title: Measure and reason about the failed layer
sections.body: --write-out prints transport timing after the request; -o /dev/null discards the body in this diagnostic. An HTTP status of 000 is not a server status: no HTTP response was received. Inspect hostname resolution separately when using a domain.
sections.code:
curl -sS -o /dev/null --max-time 5 \
  -w 'status=%{http_code} connect=%{time_connect}s total=%{time_total}s\n' \
  http://127.0.0.1:8080/healthz
sections.walkthrough: This timing command does not use --fail-with-body, so an HTTP 500 can still have curl status zero. Check both the printed HTTP status and the process outcome. Avoid -k as a default fix for TLS errors; correct the hostname and trust configuration.

takeaway: Check transport errors, HTTP status and response body separately. Bound diagnostic requests and preserve the failed layer before deciding whether the problem is routing, TLS, a handler or a downstream dependency.
reviewAnswer: Returns nonzero for HTTP errors and retains the body
question: What does curl --fail-with-body add for HTTP 4xx or 5xx?
wrongAnswers: It retries every POST until it succeeds
It disables certificate verification
hint: A transport success can still carry an HTTP error.
nuance: Do not assume curl exit status zero means the application returned HTTP 200.

title: A Go service on Linux: systemctl and journalctl
objective: Inspect a systemd service, follow its logs and understand its restart boundary.
introduction: A native Go binary can run directly under a service manager; Kubernetes is not required. These examples assume Linux with systemd and a preinstalled go-api.service. They do not apply to macOS launchd or every container environment.

sections.title: Read the unit and its current state
sections.body: systemctl cat shows the installed unit and drop-ins. status includes active state and recent log context; show exposes selected properties. Verify the executable and service user before changing the process lifecycle.
sections.code:
systemctl cat go-api.service
systemctl status go-api.service --no-pager
systemctl show go-api.service -p MainPID -p ActiveState -p SubState
sections.walkthrough: An inactive or failed status can produce a nonzero exit code. Check ExecStart, WorkingDirectory and User in the unit. Unit content may reveal configuration paths; inspect only the required evidence before sharing logs.

sections.title: Follow the unit log instead of guessing a file path
sections.body: journalctl selects journal entries for a unit and time range. -f follows new entries; Ctrl-C stops following without stopping the service. Access may require membership or administrator permissions depending on the host configuration.
sections.code:
journalctl -u go-api.service --since "10 minutes ago" --no-pager
journalctl -u go-api.service -n 50 --no-pager
journalctl -u go-api.service -f
sections.walkthrough: Correlate startup, request errors and shutdown timestamps. A missing journal permission is different from no application logs. The program should emit useful stdout/stderr records without credentials or full sensitive request payloads.

sections.title: Restart the intended service and verify recovery
sections.body: daemon-reload reloads unit definitions after editing them; it does not restart a process by itself. restart replaces the running service and can interrupt traffic. An ordinary deployment needs a deliberate change window and an application shutdown budget.
sections.code:
# After an intentional unit-file change on your own host:
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl restart go-api.service
systemctl is-active go-api.service
curl --max-time 5 --fail-with-body http://127.0.0.1:8080/healthz
sections.walkthrough: These two sudo commands mutate host state and need authorization on that machine. Verify both service state and HTTP behavior. A running process can still be unhealthy; repeated restarts can conceal a bad configuration instead of repairing it.

takeaway: Inspect the unit, state and journal before restarting. Reloading definitions and replacing a process are distinct actions; verify the application endpoint after a controlled service change.
reviewAnswer: Reloads unit definitions without restarting the service
question: What does systemctl daemon-reload do?
wrongAnswers: It rotates all application passwords
It restarts every Go process immediately
hint: Unit configuration and process lifetime are separate.
nuance: The service manager can report active while the application endpoint is failing.

title: Build a small Go image with explicit runtime needs
objective: Separate the build stage from the runtime image and identify what a minimal image leaves out.
introduction: A container image packages a native application and its runtime files. It does not compile Go inside the iOS app, and it does not remove the need to maintain the operating environment. Multi-stage builds let the final image omit the compiler and source tree.

sections.title: Read the two stages
sections.body: The builder resolves dependencies and compiles a Linux binary. The final stage copies only the program. This example assumes go.mod and go.sum exist and the program lives in cmd/api.
sections.code:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM golang:1.27 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN go mod download
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=linux go build -o /out/api ./cmd/api

FROM scratch
COPY --from=build /out/api /api
USER 65532:65532
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["/api"]
sections.walkthrough: This scratch example fits a compatible pure-Go binary with no required external files. It omits CA certificates, zoneinfo, a shell and writable application directories. Add the actual runtime assets or choose an appropriate maintained runtime base. Pin and update base image digests in a reproducible release process.

sections.title: Build the final image and inspect its metadata
sections.body: Keep logs, local builds and secrets out of the build context with .dockerignore. Copy module files before source to reuse dependency work. The actual final image still needs a startup test; metadata inspection alone cannot prove its runtime files are sufficient.
sections.code:
docker build -t go-api:dev .
docker image inspect go-api:dev --format '{{.Config.User}} {{json .Config.Entrypoint}}'
docker image ls go-api
sections.walkthrough: For this Dockerfile the user should be 65532:65532 and the entrypoint /api. Verify the build succeeds before inspecting the tag, or you might inspect an older image. A CGO-dependent program needs a compatible build/runtime strategy.

sections.title: Run the artifact you intend to release
sections.body: A non-root user reduces ordinary process privileges, but does not replace resource and filesystem limits. Test startup, configuration, TLS requirements and graceful termination using the actual final image. A compiler-stage unit test alone cannot prove the minimal runtime image contains the files the service needs.

takeaway: Build with the toolchain, run with the required runtime files, and verify the final image. A smaller image must still satisfy the program's contract.
reviewAnswer: Can omit the compiler from the runtime image
question: Which statement is correct about a multi-stage image build?
wrongAnswers: It makes every Go dependency work without cgo
It guarantees scratch contains certificates and time-zone data
hint: List the runtime files before choosing scratch as a base image.
nuance: A static executable may still need certificates, configuration, zoneinfo or writable storage.

title: Docker daily commands: build, run, inspect and stop
objective: Run a named local container and diagnose it with logs, inspect and stats.
introduction: Start with a trusted project containing the Dockerfile from the earlier lesson and a Go service listening on :8080. The following commands use an isolated development container named go-api-dev; an image, a container instance and a published port are different objects.

sections.title: Build once and start a named instance
sections.body: build tags the image produced from the current context. run creates a container; -d runs it in the background and -p publishes a container port at a host address. Bind the host side to loopback when the exercise should stay local.
sections.code:
docker build -t go-api:dev .
docker run -d --name go-api-dev \
  -p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080 -e APP_ENV=development go-api:dev
docker ps --filter name=go-api-dev
curl --max-time 5 --fail-with-body http://127.0.0.1:8080/healthz
sections.walkthrough: Run only after the build succeeds and choose another name or port if already used. The Go listener must accept container-interface traffic, usually :8080. EXPOSE in the Dockerfile alone does not publish anything on the host.

sections.title: Inspect the instance and its actual runtime
sections.body: logs reads stdout/stderr, inspect can select one property, and stats reports current resource usage. docker exec starts a new command inside the container; a scratch image has no sh, ls or other debugging utility unless you explicitly supplied one.
sections.code:
docker logs --tail 50 go-api-dev
docker inspect --format '{{.State.Status}} {{.State.ExitCode}}' go-api-dev
docker stats --no-stream go-api-dev
sections.walkthrough: A stopped container is omitted by ordinary ps; use docker ps -a when investigating an exit. ExitCode is not an HTTP status. Avoid dumping all inspect properties when only state is needed because configuration can include sensitive environment data.

sections.title: Stop and remove only this instance
sections.body: stop sends a graceful termination signal and allows a finite timeout before forced termination. rm removes the stopped container, not the image or unrelated volumes. Replacing an image tag does not upgrade a previously created container.
sections.code:
docker stop --timeout 15 go-api-dev
docker ps -a --filter name=go-api-dev
docker rm go-api-dev
docker image inspect go-api:dev --format '{{.Id}}'
sections.walkthrough: Confirm you no longer need the disposable instance before removing it. Persistent state belongs in deliberate storage; removing the container should not be your only backup strategy. Keep the image if you want to reproduce its startup.

takeaway: Build an artifact, create a named instance and verify it through the published port. Inspect its own logs and exit state, then stop it deliberately; image tags and container instances have separate lifecycles.
reviewAnswer: No; host publication needs a runtime port mapping
question: Does EXPOSE 8080 alone make a container port reachable on the host?
wrongAnswers: Yes, it always opens a public host listener
It only works if every process runs as root
hint: Image metadata is different from host networking.
nuance: The answer is no: publication requires an explicit runtime networking configuration.

title: Compose: run an API and Redis as one local stack
objective: Read compose.yaml and use config, up, ps, logs, exec and down.
introduction: Compose defines a local multi-container environment in one file. This example assumes your API reads REDIS_ADDR, listens on :8080 and tolerates transient downstream failures. Use a disposable directory for the exercise and save the file below as compose.yaml.

sections.title: Describe services and readiness in the file
sections.body: Service names provide network discovery on the Compose network. The API connects to redis:6379, not its own localhost. A dependency health check orders initial startup; it does not guarantee Redis stays healthy, so the Go client still needs deadlines and recovery.
sections.code:
services:
  api:
    build: .
    ports: ["127.0.0.1:8080:8080"]
    environment:
      REDIS_ADDR: redis:6379
    depends_on:
      redis:
        condition: service_healthy
  redis:
    image: redis:8-alpine
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 5
sections.walkthrough: This intentionally disposable Redis has no persistent volume or public port. Choose a supported tested image version for your project and pin release digests when needed. The API Dockerfile must exist in the same build context.

sections.title: Validate, start and inspect the project
sections.body: -p gives the stack a predictable project name. config --quiet validates without printing resolved configuration. up --build -d builds and starts; ps and logs reveal readiness and startup errors. Use the same project name for each command.
sections.code:
docker compose -p go-lab config --quiet
docker compose -p go-lab up --build -d
docker compose -p go-lab ps
docker compose -p go-lab logs --tail 50 api redis
sections.walkthrough: Configuration validation does not prove the images will build or the service will boot. A missing Dockerfile, unavailable image or failing Redis health check each needs its own fix. Avoid publishing the full resolved config if it includes secrets.

sections.title: Probe a dependency and tear down deliberately
sections.body: exec runs inside an existing service container; redis-cli PING checks the Redis protocol path. down stops and removes the project containers and its normal networks. It does not delete named volumes unless requested with an additional destructive option.
sections.code:
docker compose -p go-lab exec redis redis-cli PING
curl --max-time 5 --fail-with-body http://127.0.0.1:8080/healthz
docker compose -p go-lab down
sections.walkthrough: PING should return PONG, while the HTTP check verifies your API route. Run down only when the local session is finished. This fixture uses ephemeral Redis storage, so its data goes away with the disposable container.

takeaway: Use service DNS names inside a Compose network, validate the file and inspect each service. Initial dependency ordering complements application retry/deadline behavior; it does not replace it.
reviewAnswer: Lets api reach Redis at redis:6379 in this stack
question: Where should this Compose API connect to Redis?
wrongAnswers: 127.0.0.1:6379 inside the API container
The Dockerfile EXPOSE instruction as a hostname
hint: Each container has its own loopback address.
nuance: A startup health check is not a guarantee of future dependency availability.

title: Container storage: bind mounts, volumes and permissions
objective: Choose a mount for configuration or persistent state and inspect it without deleting data.
introduction: A container writable layer usually disappears when its instance is removed. A bind mount maps a host path; a named volume has a lifecycle managed by the container runtime. These local examples use a dedicated fixture and Redis to demonstrate the difference.

sections.title: Mount a configuration file read-only
sections.body: A bind mount exposes a host path to the container. --mount makes source, destination and read-only intent explicit. The example assumes ./config.json already exists and the API accepts a -config flag; adapt that flag to your own program.
sections.code:
docker run --rm --name go-api-config \
  --mount "type=bind,source=$PWD/config.json,target=/etc/go-api/config.json,readonly" \
  go-api:dev -config /etc/go-api/config.json
sections.walkthrough: Unlike some -v forms, --mount reports a missing source instead of silently making a directory. The image must let its configured user read the file. On macOS, file sharing also crosses the container VM boundary.

sections.title: Give disposable Redis a separate data volume
sections.body: Create a dedicated named volume and mount it at Redis data storage. Append-only persistence records writes into that volume; it does not create an off-host backup. The port remains private to this container unless you publish it separately.
sections.code:
docker volume create go-lab-data
docker run -d --name go-lab-redis \
  --mount type=volume,source=go-lab-data,target=/data \
  redis:8-alpine redis-server --appendonly yes
docker exec go-lab-redis redis-cli SET example hello
sections.walkthrough: Use an unused container name. SET changes only this exercise Redis key. The volume survives removal of the container; persistence and restore procedures still need testing against the selected Redis version.

sections.title: Remove an instance without deleting its stored data
sections.body: Inspect mounts to confirm storage identity, then stop and remove only the Redis instance. The volume remains available for a later explicitly configured container. Avoid prune or rm -v as a casual repair for a service that owns important state.
sections.code:
docker inspect --format '{{json .Mounts}}' go-lab-redis
docker stop go-lab-redis
docker rm go-lab-redis
docker volume inspect go-lab-data
sections.walkthrough: The final command should still find the named volume. A missing container is expected after rm. Delete the exercise volume later only when you intentionally no longer need its data and have checked its exact name.

takeaway: Container replacement, volume deletion and backup are separate operations. Use explicit mount paths, account for the service UID and verify storage identity before changing the lifecycle of stateful workloads.
reviewAnswer: Can survive removal of the container using it
question: What normally happens to a named volume after docker rm without volume-removal flags?
wrongAnswers: It is always erased together with the image
It is automatically backed up to your Git remote
hint: A volume has its own lifecycle.
nuance: Surviving replacement does not protect a volume against host loss or deliberate deletion.

title: Docker and Podman: images are not running containers
objective: Distinguish image, container, host networking and persistent data while comparing local runtimes.
introduction: Docker and Podman can build and run OCI-style container images, but their host integration, daemon model, networking and rootless behavior are not identical. An image is an artifact; a container is a running or stopped instance with its own lifecycle.

sections.title: Read build and run separately
sections.body: These Podman commands build an image from a trusted project and start one named container. The published port is restricted to the local host in this development example. Docker has similar basic commands, but do not assume every option and host behavior is interchangeable.
sections.code:
podman build -t localhost/go-api:dev .
podman run --rm --name go-api \
  -p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080 localhost/go-api:dev
sections.walkthrough: The application inside the container must listen on an appropriate container interface, usually :8080, for port forwarding to reach it. Its own localhost is not the host's localhost. --rm removes this disposable container on exit; it does not manage external persistent data.

sections.title: Inspect rootless runtime and the container VM
sections.body: Podman info reports the active environment; select only the rootless field when that is what you need. On macOS and Windows, Podman commonly uses a Linux VM. machine list and machine start manage that VM rather than the individual application container.
sections.code:
podman info --format '{{.Host.Security.Rootless}}'
# On macOS/Windows with an existing Podman machine:
podman machine list
# Start the chosen existing machine only if it is stopped:
podman machine start
sections.walkthrough: Linux installations may not use a Podman machine at all. Rootless does not mean unlimited host access or identical Docker networking. Inspect the selected connection and VM state before creating or restarting any shared environment.

sections.title: Inspect logs and stop the intended instance
sections.body: Run these in a second terminal while the earlier foreground go-api container is running. logs reads its stdout/stderr, ps selects its state and stop requests graceful termination. The earlier --rm option removes the disposable container on exit.
sections.code:
podman ps --filter name=go-api
podman logs --tail 50 go-api
podman stats --no-stream go-api
podman stop --time 15 go-api
sections.walkthrough: Use the exact exercise name so another service is not affected. Persistent data needs a deliberate volume and backup policy; --rm concerns the container instance, not an automatic external-storage lifecycle. The image remains available afterwards.

takeaway: Images, instances, virtual-machine integration and persistent data are different layers. Similar command names do not establish identical runtime behavior.
reviewAnswer: Refers to its network namespace, not the host
question: Which statement is correct about container localhost?
wrongAnswers: Every other container and the host at once
A public service endpoint automatically created by the runtime
hint: Identify whether an address belongs to the container, the VM or the host.
nuance: Rootless containers still need explicit resource, filesystem and network policies.

title: Publish an image: tags, digests and target platforms
objective: Tag and push an image you own, inspect its digest and match its platform to the deployment.
introduction: A cluster pulls an image from a registry it can reach; a local Docker image does not appear there automatically. Tags are mutable names, while a digest identifies specific image content. Replace the example registry and owner with a namespace where you have permission to publish.

sections.title: Authenticate without a password in the command line
sections.body: Use the registry credential flow appropriate to the host; --password-stdin keeps the token out of process arguments. This example reads a token interactively in Bash, passes it through stdin and unsets the variable after login.
sections.code:
registry=registry.example.com
read -r -s -p "Registry token: " registry_token
printf "\n"
printf "%s" "$registry_token" | docker login "$registry" \
  --username YOUR_USER --password-stdin
unset registry_token
sections.walkthrough: registry.example.com and YOUR_USER are placeholders. Do not run with shell tracing enabled or put tokens in a committed script. Docker stores credentials according to its configured credential helper; check that configuration on a shared host.

sections.title: Publish an explicit version and record the result
sections.body: Tagging gives the same local image another name; pushing uploads its referenced layers and manifest. Inspect the output digest and associate it with the source commit and tests. A tag called tested is still mutable unless the registry enforces otherwise.
sections.code:
image=registry.example.com/YOUR_OWNER/go-api:0.1.0
docker tag go-api:dev "$image"
docker push "$image"
docker image inspect "$image" --format '{{json .RepoDigests}}'
sections.walkthrough: Replace owner and registry first and publish only your intended artifact. The digest from a successful push identifies the remote content. Referencing image@sha256:... in a deployment avoids relying on a mutable tag; use the full real digest, not an ellipsis.

sections.title: Match the image platform to the target nodes
sections.body: Buildx can build for a specified target when the builder supports it. A multi-platform image requires compatible toolchains, base images and code for each target. Setting GOOS alone does not ensure the native CPU architecture matches the Kubernetes node.
sections.code:
docker buildx ls
docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64 \
  -t registry.example.com/YOUR_OWNER/go-api:0.1.0-amd64 --push .
docker buildx imagetools inspect registry.example.com/YOUR_OWNER/go-api:0.1.0-amd64
sections.walkthrough: This command publishes a separate amd64 tag. A compatible buildx builder may need emulation or native nodes. The earlier Dockerfile compiles inside its selected builder platform; custom cross-compilation needs explicit GOARCH/TARGETARCH handling.

takeaway: Publish to an owned registry namespace, retain the pushed digest and verify the target platform. A local tag or a successful host build does not prove a cluster can pull and run that artifact.
reviewAnswer: Identifies image content more precisely than a mutable tag
question: Why record a registry image digest for a release?
wrongAnswers: A tag can never be updated once pushed
A digest provides database backups automatically
hint: Names and content identities are different.
nuance: A digest identifies content; platform compatibility and pull authorization still need verification.

title: kubectl first steps: context, namespace and permissions
objective: Inspect the target cluster and explicitly scope commands before making changes.
introduction: kubectl reads a kubeconfig and sends requests to its selected cluster as a configured identity. A namespace narrows many workload operations but does not select a cluster. These lessons assume an existing disposable development cluster with a context named dev-cluster; substitute your actual development context.

sections.title: Identify the context before querying workloads
sections.body: config get-contexts lists saved contexts, and current-context prints the default. A context bundles cluster, identity and an optional namespace. These commands inspect local configuration; they do not establish whether the remote API is reachable.
sections.code:
kubectl config get-contexts
kubectl config current-context
kubectl --context dev-cluster cluster-info
sections.walkthrough: Replace dev-cluster with the development context you inspected. Avoid config view --raw in shared output because it can reveal credentials. Supplying --context on later commands avoids silently targeting a different default cluster.

sections.title: Find namespaces and discover resource types
sections.body: get namespaces shows available namespaces when your identity is allowed to list them. api-resources tells you the kinds the server exposes. auth can-i checks authorization for one requested action; it is not a proof that the action will otherwise succeed.
sections.code:
kubectl --context dev-cluster get namespaces
kubectl --context dev-cluster api-resources --namespaced=true
kubectl --context dev-cluster auth can-i create deployments -n go-lab
sections.walkthrough: A no response from can-i means your identity lacks that permission. An absent go-lab namespace must be created deliberately by an authorized user before the later exercises. Do not switch to a more privileged production credential as an automatic workaround.

sections.title: Scope a development namespace explicitly
sections.body: Create go-lab only on the inspected development cluster if it does not exist. -n selects the namespace for the request. Pod queries can be watched with -w; Ctrl-C stops watching without deleting any workload.
sections.code:
# One-time setup if go-lab does not exist:
kubectl --context dev-cluster create namespace go-lab
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab get pods -o wide
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab get pods -w
sections.walkthrough: An empty namespace correctly reports no resources. AlreadyExists from create means the setup already happened; inspect before reusing a namespace someone else owns. Namespace deletion later would delete its namespaced resources, so it is not a casual cleanup command.

takeaway: Know the context, identity and namespace before working on a cluster. Keep the development context and namespace explicit in commands; a namespace flag alone cannot protect against targeting the wrong cluster.
reviewAnswer: Selects the kubeconfig context for one invocation
question: What does kubectl --context select for one invocation?
wrongAnswers: --namespace changes both the cluster and identity
--all-namespaces grants administrator privileges
hint: A context includes the cluster and user identity.
nuance: Authorization and reachability are separate checks; a context name alone is not proof of the intended server.

title: Kubernetes reconciles a workload; a Service routes to it
objective: Read Deployment, Pod labels, resource budgets and a Service without confusing them with an application build.
introduction: Kubernetes operates containerized workloads. It does not write your Go code or remove distributed-system failures. A Deployment describes the desired replicated workload; a Service gives selected Pods a stable network abstraction while individual Pods are replaced.

sections.title: Follow selectors and labels
sections.body: This abbreviated manifest connects a Service to Pods carrying app: go-api. The image reference is a placeholder for an image you have built, tested and published to an accessible registry. Read it as configuration, not something the iOS app can apply.
sections.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: go-api
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels: {app: go-api}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: {app: go-api}
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: your-registry/go-api:tested
          ports: [{containerPort: 8080}]
          resources:
            requests: {cpu: "100m", memory: "128Mi"}
            limits: {cpu: "1", memory: "512Mi"}
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: go-api
spec:
  selector: {app: go-api}
  ports: [{port: 80, targetPort: 8080}]
sections.walkthrough: The numbers illustrate syntax, not capacity recommendations. This Service is internal by default; public ingress, TLS and authentication need their own design. The Deployment example still needs suitable probe and shutdown policies.

sections.title: Observe replicas, requests and limits
sections.body: Requests influence scheduling; CPU and memory limits have different runtime effects. Use the Pod specification and Deployment state to inspect the declared budget, then compare with metrics if the cluster exposes them. The sample numbers are illustrative rather than recommendations.
sections.code:
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab get deployment go-api
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab get pods -l app=go-api -o wide
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab get deployment go-api \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].resources}{"\n"}'
sections.walkthrough: Run after the context/setup and apply lessons. Two replicas each allowing fifty downstream calls can present a hundred simultaneous calls. Resource declarations do not measure actual usage; memory exhaustion can terminate a container while CPU limits can throttle it.

sections.title: Use orchestration only when it pays for itself
sections.body: Rolling replacement and service discovery help teams operating many workloads, but cluster maintenance and debugging cost time. A VM, a managed service or a single container host can be simpler for a small application. Learn the reconciliation model before copying a large production manifest, and inspect a plan in a non-production environment before applying it.

takeaway: Match labels to selectors, give each replica a resource and downstream budget, and treat public routing as a separate concern.
reviewAnswer: Chooses matching Pod labels for stable routing
question: Which statement is correct about a kubernetes service selector?
wrongAnswers: By reading the package name of the Go executable
By compiling every image named in the cluster
hint: Trace Deployment selector, Pod label and Service selector together.
nuance: Scaling replicas also scales their downstream connection pools and worker pressure.

title: Deploy a manifest: explain, dry-run, diff and apply
objective: Validate a workload document and observe reconciliation rather than assuming apply means ready.
introduction: A manifest declares desired state; the API accepting it is only the start of reconciliation. Save the earlier Deployment and Service example as deployment.yaml, set a real pullable image reference and use the go-lab development namespace from the context lesson.

sections.title: Read the schema and validate with the server
sections.body: explain documents a field from the API schema. apply --dry-run=server asks the server to validate and default the request without persisting it. It still requires API access and appropriate permission and can depend on admission configuration.
sections.code:
kubectl --context dev-cluster explain deployment.spec.template.spec.containers
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab apply \
  --dry-run=server -f deployment.yaml
sections.walkthrough: Fix unknown fields and validation errors before the real apply. A successful dry run does not schedule Pods, pull images or test your application. Only submit trusted reviewed files, including any resource namespace declared inside them.

sections.title: Review the delta and apply the intended state
sections.body: diff compares the proposed object with live state; exit one means differences, not necessarily a failed comparison. apply persists the desired resource changes, so inspect the exact files and target namespace before this mutation.
sections.code:
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab diff -f deployment.yaml
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab apply -f deployment.yaml
sections.walkthrough: kubectl diff uses status zero for no changes, one for differences and greater than one for errors. Do not hide all nonzero codes with || true in automation. apply may create or update several documents from this file.

sections.title: Wait for convergence and inspect the resulting objects
sections.body: rollout status waits for a Deployment update to finish within a timeout. get reports objects and their current state; it does not prove every business request succeeds. A timeout should lead to diagnosis of the existing rollout before another deployment attempt.
sections.code:
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab rollout status deploy/go-api --timeout=120s
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab get deploy,rs,pods,svc -l app=go-api
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab get svc go-api
sections.walkthrough: The original Service example does not give the Service object an app label, so the final explicit Service query is necessary. Inspect readiness, image pulls and events if convergence fails. A successful apply alone is not release success.

takeaway: Validate a reviewed document, understand diff exit codes, apply once and observe the rollout. API acceptance and a ready, functional application are separate milestones.
reviewAnswer: Means live state differs from the proposed manifest
question: What does kubectl diff returning exit status 1 normally mean?
wrongAnswers: The manifest was successfully deployed
The cluster has exactly one failed Pod
hint: A visible difference is an intended diff outcome.
nuance: Dry-run validates a request but does not test image availability or scheduling.

title: Debug Pods: get, describe, logs, events and top
objective: Find the concrete reason behind Pending, CrashLoopBackOff or an unready container.
introduction: Read the workload state before changing it. A Deployment, a Pod and a container can each have a different status, so diagnose the layer that is failing. These commands refer to the earlier go-api Deployment in the explicit go-lab development namespace.

sections.title: Find the Pod and read its events
sections.body: get -o wide includes node and Pod addresses. describe exposes scheduling decisions, container state and recent events. Copy the exact Pod name from get rather than inventing an identifier; the placeholder below must be replaced.
sections.code:
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab get pods -l app=go-api -o wide
pod_name=REPLACE_WITH_ACTUAL_POD
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab describe pod "$pod_name"
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab get events --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp
sections.walkthrough: Pending often needs scheduling/volume evidence; ImagePullBackOff needs the image or registry failure. CrashLoopBackOff describes retry backoff after container failure, not a root cause. Check the reported reason and exit code first.

sections.title: Read the right container and the previous attempt
sections.body: logs reads application stdout/stderr. -c selects the container name api from the earlier manifest. --previous requests the last terminated instance when one exists, which is valuable when the current container restarted before you could follow it.
sections.code:
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab logs "$pod_name" -c api --tail=100
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab logs "$pod_name" -c api --previous --tail=100
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab logs "$pod_name" -c api -f --since=5m
sections.walkthrough: No previous container is a valid reason for --previous to fail. Ctrl-C only stops following logs. Redact sensitive application data before sharing output and correlate timestamps with restarts and rollout events.

sections.title: Inspect resources and choose an available debug path
sections.body: top requires the cluster metrics API, commonly provided by Metrics Server. exec starts a command that already exists in the image; the earlier scratch Go image has no shell. For richer diagnosis, use an approved ephemeral debug image and the required cluster permissions.
sections.code:
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab top pods -l app=go-api
kubectl --context dev-cluster top nodes
# Only for an image that actually contains /bin/sh:
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab exec -it "$pod_name" -c api -- /bin/sh
sections.walkthrough: A missing metrics API does not mean resource usage is zero. The exec line will fail for scratch images by design; use logs, profiles or a deliberate debug-container workflow instead of assuming every production image includes utilities.

takeaway: Read exact state, events, container logs and resource evidence before restarting. Previous logs can explain a crash loop; missing metrics or a missing shell is a tooling boundary, not an application diagnosis.
reviewAnswer: Reads logs from the previous terminated container instance
question: Which logs can --previous retrieve for a restarted container?
wrongAnswers: All logs from every deleted Pod forever
Only HTTP requests from the host browser
hint: A restarted container has a previous instance.
nuance: Container logs and events have retention limits; use centralized collection for durable history.

title: Service routing: selectors, endpoints and port-forward
objective: Trace a request from a local port through a Service to a ready application endpoint.
introduction: A Service object can exist while routing to no useful Pods. Diagnose its selector, selected endpoints, target port and application listener separately. This lesson uses the earlier internal Service go-api on port 80 targeting the Go container port 8080.

sections.title: Check selector and ready endpoints
sections.body: A Service selector matches Pod labels; EndpointSlices describe backend addresses and readiness. Deployment existence alone does not prove the Service selected its Pods. Query the named Service because the sample object does not have an app metadata label.
sections.code:
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab describe service go-api
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab get pods -l app=go-api --show-labels
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab get endpointslices \
  -l kubernetes.io/service-name=go-api -o wide
sections.walkthrough: Empty endpoints suggest a selector mismatch, missing Pods or readiness problems. Compare targetPort 8080 with the actual Go listener. A listener bound to 127.0.0.1 inside the Pod cannot normally serve traffic arriving at its Pod interface.

sections.title: Forward one local port and make a bounded request
sections.body: port-forward supplies a temporary local development path; it is not a public ingress or load test. Bind it to loopback and keep the process running while you use a second terminal to call the local address.
sections.code:
# Terminal 1; stop with Ctrl-C:
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab port-forward \
  --address 127.0.0.1 service/go-api 8080:80
# Terminal 2:
curl --max-time 5 --fail-with-body http://127.0.0.1:8080/healthz
sections.walkthrough: The local 8080 forwards to Service port 80, which resolves to a Pod target. If another local process owns 8080, choose a different local port. The session can end when its selected Pod disappears; it does not create durable routing.

sections.title: Distinguish application access from a diagnostic tunnel
sections.body: An in-cluster client in go-lab can normally resolve go-api; a client in another namespace can use go-api.go-lab.svc.cluster.local on a cluster using that DNS suffix. Network policy and DNS configuration still apply. A port-forward does not prove the ordinary in-cluster network route works.
sections.code:
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab get service go-api -o yaml
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab get networkpolicy
sections.walkthrough: Check Service type, ports and selectors in the first output. No policies in this namespace is not a complete security audit: cluster networking and other policy mechanisms can also affect traffic. Ingress, public TLS and authentication need their own configuration.

takeaway: Trace labels, endpoint readiness, Service ports and the listener as separate links. Port-forward is a useful temporary tunnel, but it cannot validate all normal service-network and public-ingress behavior.
reviewAnswer: Creates a temporary local tunnel, not public ingress
question: What does port-forward create in this development example?
wrongAnswers: A permanent load balancer for all internet clients
A new container image with DNS installed
hint: The local forwarding process has a lifetime.
nuance: A tunnel request can succeed while the normal network-policy path still fails.

title: Configuration: ConfigMaps, Secrets and update behavior
objective: Create a non-secret setting, mount a Secret reference and understand why environment changes need replacement.
introduction: Separate application configuration from the image artifact. ConfigMaps hold ordinary configuration; Secrets are intended for sensitive values but are not made confidential merely by base64 encoding. These development examples assume a namespace you own and the permissions to manage its configuration.

sections.title: Generate and apply a non-secret ConfigMap
sections.body: create with --dry-run=client -o yaml generates an object locally. Piping that object to apply creates or updates the named configuration on the explicit cluster. LOG_LEVEL is an ordinary non-secret value here, so showing its key is appropriate.
sections.code:
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab create configmap go-api-config \
  --from-literal=LOG_LEVEL=info --dry-run=client -o yaml | \
  kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab apply -f -
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab describe configmap go-api-config
sections.walkthrough: In a Bash script, enable pipefail and handle the pipeline status. The first command only generates YAML; the second performs the API mutation. Do not use a ConfigMap for a database password or access token.

sections.title: Reference existing config and secret keys from the Pod
sections.body: This is a fragment to merge into the api container in deployment.yaml, not a standalone manifest. It assumes an existing go-api-credentials Secret with a password key, supplied through your cluster secret-management process.
sections.code:
env:
  - name: LOG_LEVEL
    valueFrom:
      configMapKeyRef:
        name: go-api-config
        key: LOG_LEVEL
  - name: DB_PASSWORD
    valueFrom:
      secretKeyRef:
        name: go-api-credentials
        key: password
sections.walkthrough: The application reads these values when its process starts. Restrict Secret access and configure storage protection at the cluster level. Never commit live Secret YAML or paste decoded credentials into a lesson exercise.

sections.title: Replace Pods when environment configuration changes
sections.body: Changing the ConfigMap does not rewrite environment variables in a running process. A controlled rollout restart replaces Pods so they read the updated values. ConfigMap volume updates have different propagation and application-reload behavior, and subPath mounts do not receive normal automatic updates.
sections.code:
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab rollout restart deployment/go-api
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab rollout status deployment/go-api --timeout=120s
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab get pods -l app=go-api
sections.walkthrough: Only restart after the reviewed configuration and Pod template are ready. Observe readiness and service behavior afterwards without logging the password. This restart changes running workloads; it is not a read-only configuration check.

takeaway: Use ConfigMaps for ordinary values and controlled Secret references for credentials. Environment is captured at process startup; replacing Pods and reloading mounted files are distinct update strategies.
reviewAnswer: Is captured when the container process starts
question: When does a process receive a ConfigMap-backed environment variable?
wrongAnswers: Every time kubectl get pods is called
Immediately whenever any Secret in the cluster changes
hint: A running process keeps its environment.
nuance: Base64 is an encoding, not encryption or an access-control policy.

title: Readiness, liveness and graceful shutdown
objective: Give each health signal one purpose and arrange a bounded stop that drains owned work.
introduction: A process being alive does not mean it can accept useful work. Readiness controls whether a Pod receives normal Service traffic. Liveness can trigger a restart. A startup probe can allow initialization before the other probes take effect. Choose each signal according to the failure it should detect.

sections.title: Give each probe one action
sections.body: Merge this fragment into the api container only if the Go server implements these endpoints. Readiness gates normal Service traffic; liveness should detect a condition a restart can repair. A startup probe delays the other probes until startup succeeds.
sections.walkthrough: The intervals are examples, not universal budgets. A shared Redis outage should not make every liveness endpoint fail and restart all replicas. Readiness should reflect the service degraded-mode contract; test the actual handler behavior.

sections.title: Drain requests within a finite deadline
sections.body: This native Go fragment assumes srv is already serving in another goroutine. The signal context requests shutdown; a separate context bounds draining so an already-canceled signal context does not abort it immediately.
sections.walkthrough: Ten seconds is illustrative and must fit the platform termination grace period. Shutdown does not automatically wait for every background worker or hijacked connection. Stop accepting work, signal owned workers, join them, and close shared clients in a deliberate order.

sections.title: Test the termination path under traffic
sections.body: Readiness changes and endpoint propagation take time; applications can still see late requests. Make handlers safe during draining, choose how to reject new work, and verify existing requests finish or fail predictably. Persist required background work before exit. Probe intervals and thresholds should fit startup and recovery behavior instead of creating a rapid restart loop.

takeaway: A health check needs an action model: route traffic, wait for startup, or restart. Graceful shutdown requires explicit ownership, deadlines and a tested drain path.
reviewAnswer: Readiness gates traffic; liveness can trigger a restart
question: Which statement is correct about readiness and liveness?
wrongAnswers: Liveness, because every dependency failure must restart the Pod
A CPU profile taken once when the image was built
hint: For each health failure, name the action the platform should take.
nuance: Use a fresh bounded drain context; the signal context is already canceled when shutdown starts.

title: Release operations: rollout, scale and rollback
objective: Change an image deliberately, observe revisions and understand what rollback cannot restore.
introduction: A Deployment rollout changes its Pod template and replaces replicas under its update policy. A timeout or unhealthy Pod requires investigation before further mutations. These examples operate only on the inspected development go-api Deployment, using a real tested image reference in place of the placeholder.

sections.title: Inspect history and set the intended artifact
sections.body: rollout history lists retained Deployment revisions. set image changes the api container image in the Pod template. Use an immutable image digest in a real release where reproducibility matters, and keep the declarative source in sync with this operational change.
sections.code:
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab rollout history deployment/go-api
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab set image deployment/go-api \
  api=registry.example.com/YOUR_OWNER/go-api:0.1.1
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab rollout status deployment/go-api --timeout=120s
sections.walkthrough: Replace the registry, owner and version with a published tested artifact before running. set image mutates the cluster immediately. A future apply from an old manifest can overwrite the change; version-controlled deployment configuration should describe the intended final state.

sections.title: Scale with resource and downstream budgets in mind
sections.body: scale changes desired replicas, not the size of an individual process. Check workload state and pressure afterwards. Requests, limits, database pools and worker concurrency multiply across replicas; an autoscaler or another controller may subsequently change the count.
sections.code:
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab scale deployment/go-api --replicas=3
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab get deployment go-api
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab get pods -l app=go-api
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab top pods -l app=go-api
sections.walkthrough: Three replicas are a syntax example, not a capacity recommendation. top requires a metrics API. Confirm the cluster can schedule the workload and downstream systems can handle its multiplied demand rather than treating replica count as free capacity.

sections.title: Roll back a Pod template, then verify the service
sections.body: undo uses a retained earlier Deployment revision. It can restore the Pod template, but cannot reverse a database migration, external side effect or independently changed Secret/ConfigMap. Inspect the selected history revision and its artifact before a deliberate rollback.
sections.code:
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab rollout history deployment/go-api
# After selecting and reviewing an appropriate previous revision:
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab rollout undo deployment/go-api
kubectl --context dev-cluster -n go-lab rollout status deployment/go-api --timeout=120s
sections.walkthrough: The undo line chooses the previous retained revision; use --to-revision with an inspected real number for an explicit choice. Afterwards verify readiness, logs and the API through a fresh test request. Do not repeatedly undo merely because a status command timed out.

takeaway: Record the released image, observe the rollout and budget replicas against downstream capacity. Rollback restores a retained workload template, not databases or every separate configuration object.
reviewAnswer: Restores a retained previous Pod template revision
question: What can Deployment rollout undo restore?
wrongAnswers: Every database write made by the new version
All deleted Secrets and persistent-volume backups
hint: A Deployment revision tracks its workload template.
nuance: History retention and backward-compatible data changes determine whether rollback can succeed.

title: Simple monolith: start with one executable
objective: Keep a small application understandable without premature service boundaries.
introduction: Keep a small application understandable without premature service boundaries. A command-line invoice tool can parse input, compute a result and print it in one process. Trace the worked Go example, then compare the benefit with the cost before applying this design to your own project.

sections.title: The design decision
sections.body: A command-line invoice tool can parse input, compute a result and print it in one process. Functions can separate these responsibilities before packages or network services become useful. One deployment is an operational choice; it does not require one giant function or prevent later modules.

sections.body: Start splitting when different responsibilities change independently or teams need ownership boundaries. A simple monolith can scale through replicas; shared mutable state and database contention still need measurement. Avoid hiding every function behind an interface.

sections.title: Build one process with explicit composition
sections.body: Keep main responsible for configuration, dependency construction, startup and graceful shutdown. Pass dependencies into handlers rather than hiding them in package globals. Place use cases behind package APIs even if there is only one executable. This retains fast local calls and a single operational unit while allowing multiple entry points later. A monolith describes deployment; it does not require a single package or prevent good isolation inside the process.

Validate cheap input before opening that transaction, avoid network calls while holding locks and roll back on every failure path. A successful HTTP response should follow the required durable commit, not precede it. If an email must eventually follow the commit, record an outbox item atomically and process it later; sending email first cannot be rolled back with the database.

sections.title: Scale only the measured bottleneck
sections.body: Measure request latency, database time, queue depth and memory before extracting services. A process can have multiple replicas and background workers while remaining a monolith, provided shared state is durable and concurrency-safe. Start by improving indexes or isolating a slow worker. If one capability later needs independent deployment, keep its existing API and extract behind that seam. Expect remote timeouts and partial failure to become new work after extraction.

title: Layered architecture: transport, application, storage
objective: Separate responsibilities without confusing logical layers with deployed tiers.
introduction: Separate responsibilities without confusing logical layers with deployed tiers. A layered service routes requests through transport, application logic and persistence. Trace the worked Go example, then compare the benefit with the cost before applying this design to your own project.

sections.title: The design decision
sections.body: A layered service routes requests through transport, application logic and persistence. Logical layers may live in the same executable. Avoid a handler bypassing validation to write directly to storage, and avoid pass-through types that only rename the next function.

sections.title: A complete Go example
sections.body: Read this program from the entry point and follow the calls shown in the diagram. The output is included at the end so you can check the behavior without a compiler.

sections.body: A feature may touch every horizontal layer, so keep mapping work proportional to the value it protects. Layering alone does not invert dependencies, create transactions or make storage replaceable. A single function is simpler for a one-off script.

sections.title: MVC is a presentation organization
sections.body: Model–View–Controller separates a model of state and behavior, a view that renders output, and a controller that translates user input into operations. A Go web handler can act as a controller and a template as the view. This does not require a database model for every view, nor does it decide whether the application is one process or many services. Keep business invariants outside presentation formatting; use html/template rather than concatenating untrusted HTML.

sections.title: Trace dependency direction through a real request
sections.body: An HTTP layer decodes a request and maps a response; an application layer executes a use case; a storage adapter persists its state. The application should receive typed intent, not an http.Request. Likewise, database rows should not automatically become public JSON. Separate request DTOs from domain values when their validation and compatibility rules differ. Avoid a layer whose only purpose is forwarding every call unchanged to another layer.

sections.title: Put the transaction around the business operation
sections.body: A transaction belongs to the complete use case, such as moving funds between accounts. Starting and committing inside each repository method makes the two balance changes independent. Pass transaction-scoped capabilities to the use case or offer one atomic domain operation. Keep validation errors distinct from infrastructure failures, and do not convert every failure into a nil result. A layered diagram does not itself establish atomicity, authorization or idempotency.

sections.title: Reduce horizontal change amplification
sections.body: If one small feature repeatedly changes controller, manager, service, repository and mapper with no distinct decision in most layers, collapse unnecessary forwarding. Organize files by feature within a layer or introduce a vertical slice. Preserve stable cross-cutting policy such as authentication at a clear boundary. Test each layer only for the behavior it owns: request mapping, business invariant or persistence contract, rather than duplicating the same happy-path assertion five times.

nuance: The selected version for one module path must satisfy the graph’s minimum requirements. go.sum records content hashes, not a request for the newest version.

strengths: Read minimal version selection and investigate a transitive upgrade without guessing.
cautions: The selected version for one module path must satisfy the graph’s minimum requirements. go.sum records content hashes, not a request for the newest version.
designGuide.cost: A graph change can raise transitive versions; review and regression-test the selected delta instead of counting edited require lines.

title: Checksums, proxies and private modules solve different problems
objective: Diagnose downloads without leaking private paths or disabling integrity checks globally.
introduction: A download failure may come from version discovery, credentials, a proxy, the checksum database or local cache integrity. Treat those as separate layers. A checksum records content identity; it neither proves the code is safe nor decides which version the dependency graph chooses.

sections.title: Inspect effective settings
sections.body: Read configuration before changing it. Private module patterns affect how the Go command consults public services; they do not log you in to a private repository. Use the environment and credential mechanisms approved for that repository, and keep tokens out of module URLs and command history.
sections.code:
go env GOPROXY GOPRIVATE GONOPROXY GONOSUMDB
go mod download -json
go mod verify
sections.walkthrough: The commands distinguish download provenance and local verification from compilation. Download JSON can contain private module paths, so inspect it locally and redact paths before sharing an incident report.

sections.title: Scope private paths narrowly
sections.body: GOPRIVATE is a pattern list for private module path prefixes. Configure a company-specific pattern in the environment of the developer shell and CI job. GOPROXY fallback with comma versus pipe has different failure behavior; choose deliberately instead of masking every proxy error with direct access.
sections.code:
# Example only: replace the organization path.
GOPRIVATE=github.com/example-company/* go mod download
sections.walkthrough: The assignment applies to this one command rather than silently altering every future shell. It still needs separately configured repository credentials and a network route to the source.

sections.title: Keep integrity and availability separate
sections.body: A checksum mismatch deserves investigation of the module version, proxy and local files. Do not teach a build to accept changed content under an existing version. go.sum can include go.mod checksums for modules whose source is not used, and it may change after tidy without representing a new executable dependency.

takeaway: Trace discovery, transport, credentials and checksums independently. Narrow private patterns and preserve integrity verification for public dependencies.
reviewAnswer: Records verified content; it does not select versions
question: What does a go.sum entry establish?
wrongAnswers: That the module has no vulnerabilities
That this module version is the newest available
hint: Integrity, authorization and dependency selection are different layers.
nuance: A checksum verifies the expected content of a version. It does not select that version, certify its behavior or establish that no vulnerability is known.

strengths: Diagnose downloads without leaking private paths or disabling integrity checks globally.
cautions: A checksum verifies the expected content of a version. It does not select that version, certify its behavior or establish that no vulnerability is known.
designGuide.cost: Private fetches need reliable credentials and transport; retaining integrity checks makes failures easier to investigate.

title: A local workspace can hide a broken release
objective: Use go.work and replace for development while checking what an independent consumer builds.
introduction: A checkout can pass because go.work supplies a sibling module or replace points to a local directory that no consumer has. That success tests the local composition, not the published module. Keep a second path that exercises the version and files a real downstream user receives.

sections.title: See the workspace and overrides
sections.body: Inspect the active workspace and replacements before comparing two machines. A local replacement changes source selection; a replace line in a dependency is not automatically inherited by its consumers. Avoid committing an absolute workstation path as a release dependency.
sections.code:
go env GOWORK
go work edit -json
go list -m -json all
sections.walkthrough: The workspace JSON lists participating module directories; the module listing shows replacements used by the build. Compare these facts before assuming a compiler or operating-system bug.

sections.title: Verify the module on its own
sections.body: Run checks with GOWORK=off from the module directory and build a small independent consumer using the intended release version. A workspace root with several modules is not equivalent to one module where ./... automatically promises to cover every sibling.
sections.code:
GOWORK=off go mod tidy
GOWORK=off go test ./...
GOWORK=off go list -m all
sections.walkthrough: These commands deliberately ignore workspace composition. If the tests now fail, the difference is actionable: a missing requirement, an unpublished API or a dependency that only existed in the workspace.

sections.title: Test migrations from both sides
sections.body: A coordinated local API change can make producer and consumer pass together while breaking older consumers. Release the producer compatibly, pin the consumer to the released version, then test that combination. Workspace convenience should not replace a compatibility matrix for separately released modules.

takeaway: Use local overrides to iterate quickly, then turn them off to test the module and its published consumer contract independently.
reviewAnswer: Can depend on unpublished local replacements
question: Why also test with GOWORK=off?
wrongAnswers: It disables all tests that touch the filesystem
It automatically publishes every workspace module
hint: Compare the local composition with a separate consumer.
nuance: GOWORK=off removes the local workspace composition. That exposes missing published requirements and APIs that only worked through sibling modules or local replacements.

strengths: Use go.work and replace for development while checking what an independent consumer builds.
cautions: GOWORK=off removes the local workspace composition. That exposes missing published requirements and APIs that only worked through sibling modules or local replacements.
designGuide.cost: Fast local iteration needs a separate isolated-consumer check to expose unpublished assumptions before release.

title: Reproduce the artifact: vendor, build tags and embedded files
objective: Check the source and assets that a clean build actually receives.
introduction: A successful build in your checkout can depend on uncommitted generated files, platform-specific source or an asset missing from the release archive. Reproducibility concerns the whole input set: toolchain, selected modules, build constraints, generated files and embedded data.

sections.title: Inspect the selected files and dependencies
sections.body: go list exposes which source and embedded files belong to the selected target. Build tags and GOOS/GOARCH can select different implementations. An import that works on your Mac may require cgo or assembly on another target; do not infer portability from a package download.
sections.code:
go list -f '{{.GoFiles}} {{.IgnoredGoFiles}} {{.EmbedFiles}}' ./...
go list -deps ./...
go env GOOS GOARCH CGO_ENABLED
sections.walkthrough: The file selection is concrete evidence for the current build configuration. Repeat it for the intended target and inspect dependency code before promising portability to a restricted runtime.

sections.title: Treat vendor as a derived dependency tree
sections.body: Regenerate vendor after reviewing a dependency change and check it with the corresponding go.mod. Vendor mode deliberately uses that tree instead of treating a full module cache as the source of truth. Toolchain and platform differences still matter.
sections.code:
go mod vendor
go test -mod=vendor ./...
go build -mod=vendor ./...
sections.walkthrough: Run these in a development checkout or clean CI worktree. If module declarations and vendor metadata disagree, regenerate from the reviewed graph rather than hand-editing copied dependency source.

sections.title: Generated and embedded inputs are release inputs
sections.body: go generate is explicit; go build does not run arbitrary generators for you. Check generated files or run a pinned generator in a defined build step. GopherForge currently does not preserve arbitrary non-Go embed assets while vendoring; learning native build commands here does not change that app limitation.

takeaway: Build the clean release input set, not just the current working tree. Verify tags, generated files and assets, and keep vendor consistent with the reviewed graph.
reviewAnswer: Runs only when explicitly requested
question: When does go build automatically run go generate?
wrongAnswers: Before every compile of a generated package
Only when the module cache is empty
hint: Distinguish an explicit generation step from compilation.
nuance: Compilation does not automatically invoke go generate. Generation is an explicit workflow step whose tool version and output need their own checks.

strengths: Check the source and assets that a clean build actually receives.
cautions: Compilation does not automatically invoke go generate. Generation is an explicit workflow step whose tool version and output need their own checks.
designGuide.cost: Vendor and generated assets increase repository and review volume; the payoff is explicit repeatable release inputs.

title: Parallel tests must own their mutable resources
objective: Find races, test caching mistakes and shared integration fixtures before scaling concurrency.
introduction: A test can pass alone and fail when other packages or subtests run at the same time. Shared database names, environment variables, ports and mutable globals turn isolated test intent into interference. Give every test its own resources, and distinguish a data race from a wider coordination bug.

sections.title: Separate three kinds of parallelism
sections.body: -p controls how many packages are built or tested concurrently; -parallel controls parallel tests within one test binary; GOMAXPROCS affects Go execution parallelism. Setting all three high can overwhelm a shared database even though each individual test uses only a few connections.
sections.code:
go test -count=1 -shuffle=on ./...
go test -race -count=1 ./...
go test -p=2 -parallel=4 ./...
sections.walkthrough: A fresh run bypasses cached test results; shuffle exposes order dependence, and the race detector observes conflicting memory accesses on executed paths. None of these alone validates distributed database invariants.

sections.title: Give temporary resources one owner
sections.body: Use t.TempDir and t.Cleanup for filesystem state. Pick an OS-assigned listener port rather than a fixed global port. A test that mutates environment or process working directory must respect the testing package restrictions around parallel execution.
sections.walkthrough: The example is a test-file fragment importing testing and os. The test owns its directory and cleanup, and explicitly stays sequential because environment changes affect the whole process.

sections.title: Test cancellation and resource release
sections.body: Assert that work exits after cancellation and that database clients, rows, bodies and temporary servers are closed. A passing result with leaked goroutines can poison later tests or exhaust CI resources. Keep a failing shuffled seed or a deterministic reproducer rather than relying on repeated lucky retries.

takeaway: Make test ownership explicit, bound package and subtest parallelism separately, and use race detection as evidence on exercised paths rather than a proof of correctness.
reviewAnswer: Need isolated fixtures and a shared capacity budget
question: What prevents tests from overloading one test database?
wrongAnswers: Increasing every pool to match the number of tests
Running with the race detector instead of managing resources
hint: Count clients, test binaries and parallel subtests together.
nuance: Package test binaries and parallel subtests share downstream capacity. Isolate fixtures and bound their combined demand; the race detector does not size a database pool.

strengths: Find races, test caching mistakes and shared integration fixtures before scaling concurrency.
cautions: Package test binaries and parallel subtests share downstream capacity. Isolate fixtures and bound their combined demand; the race detector does not size a database pool.
designGuide.cost: Isolation requires disposable fixtures and cleanup; parallelism still spends shared database and machine capacity.

title: A microbenchmark is not a capacity test
objective: Measure allocations, concurrency and tail latency without mistaking closed-loop throughput for service capacity.
introduction: An ns/op number describes one workload in one process. A production incident may instead come from pool wait, queue growth, a slow downstream service or allocation pressure. Start with the question you need to answer and preserve the workload and environment alongside the measurement.

sections.title: Repeat a focused microbenchmark
sections.body: Select one benchmark, include allocation reporting and repeat it. Keep setup outside the timed section where that matches the production operation. Optimizing a string conversion says little about the complete HTTP-to-database request unless the conversion dominates that request.
sections.code:
go test ./internal/codec -run='^$' -bench=BenchmarkEncode -benchmem -count=5
go test ./internal/codec -run='^$' -bench=BenchmarkEncode -cpu=1,2,4
sections.walkthrough: Replace the package and benchmark with real ones. Repeated measurements expose noise; CPU variants reveal scaling effects, but they do not reproduce a network load generator or a remote database.

sections.title: Make parallel measurements honest
sections.body: RunParallel measures concurrent benchmark work using a closed loop. Retain observable work, avoid sharing an unsafe buffer, and define whether the benchmark measures hits, misses or both. Report failure rate, request sizes and queue limits for a service test instead of only a flattering average.
sections.walkthrough: This is a self-contained benchmark body importing testing. It intentionally includes the allocation and validates the result; use a representative payload before comparing implementations or drawing a capacity conclusion.

sections.title: Look at the tail and overload response
sections.body: At a steady incoming arrival rate, a saturated service can build a queue even while successful completions look fast. Observe p50/p95/p99 together with errors, active requests, pool checkout time and recovery after a burst. An unbounded queue delays failure instead of creating capacity.

takeaway: Use benchmarks to answer narrow code questions, then test the complete service with an explicit arrival rate, bounded queues and tail-latency/error measurements.
reviewAnswer: Does not establish whole-service capacity
question: What can a low ns/op result prove about a database-backed API?
wrongAnswers: That its p99 stays low at any request rate
That increasing goroutines will always increase throughput
hint: Ask which delays and failures the benchmark does not include.
nuance: A microbenchmark measures its own loop and inputs. It may omit network, pool wait, queue growth and overload failures that dominate a real service.

strengths: Measure allocations, concurrency and tail latency without mistaking closed-loop throughput for service capacity.
cautions: A microbenchmark measures its own loop and inputs. It may omit network, pool wait, queue growth and overload failures that dominate a real service.
designGuide.cost: Useful measurements require representative inputs, repeated runs and separate whole-service load evidence.

title: Profile CPU, allocation and waiting as different bottlenecks
objective: Use pprof and traces to investigate latency under load instead of increasing pools blindly.
introduction: A high-latency request does not necessarily consume much CPU. It may be waiting on a mutex, scheduling, a network response or a connection pool. Capture evidence for the same workload and time window, and choose a profile that can explain the suspected delay.

sections.title: Capture a bounded benchmark profile
sections.body: CPU profiles show sampled execution time. Heap and allocation profiles answer different memory questions, so choose the sample type deliberately. Keep the test binary with its profiles and source revision; otherwise symbol names and comparisons can become misleading.
sections.code:
go test ./internal/codec -run='^$' -bench=BenchmarkEncode -cpuprofile=cpu.out -memprofile=mem.out
go tool pprof -top cpu.out
go tool pprof -sample_index=alloc_space -top mem.out
sections.walkthrough: The commands create local profile artifacts and show where time or allocated bytes accumulate in the measured benchmark. They do not show every blocked request or replace pool wait metrics from a real service.

sections.title: Trace scheduling and explicit contention
sections.body: Execution traces provide a timeline of goroutines and runtime activity. Block and mutex profiles need suitable runtime sampling configuration; collecting zero samples is not evidence that a service never waits. Profiling itself can affect the workload, so compare with the uninstrumented baseline.
sections.code:
go test ./internal/service -run TestBurst -trace=trace.out
go tool trace trace.out
go test ./internal/service -run TestBurst -blockprofile=block.out -mutexprofile=mutex.out
sections.walkthrough: Replace TestBurst with a bounded representative test. Inspect overlap among waiting, CPU work and goroutine growth before changing concurrency or blaming the garbage collector.

sections.title: Turn evidence into one falsifiable change
