sections.body: If pool checkout dominates, inspect request arrival rate and slow operations before raising pool limits. If allocation dominates, find retained objects and hot allocation sites. Expose production profiling only through an appropriately restricted diagnostic path because profiles can reveal application data and implementation details.

takeaway: Match the profile to the suspected bottleneck and compare one controlled change. CPU time, allocated bytes and waiting time are related but different measurements.
reviewAnswer: May indicate waiting, not spare request capacity
question: Why can a slow service have a mostly idle CPU?
wrongAnswers: Every slow request must consume one full core
The garbage collector always accounts for all request latency
hint: Follow where requests spend time, including queues.
nuance: A blocked request can spend most of its time waiting while consuming little CPU. Inspect queue, pool and synchronization delays as well as execution samples.

strengths: Use pprof and traces to investigate latency under load instead of increasing pools blindly.
cautions: A blocked request can spend most of its time waiting while consuming little CPU. Inspect queue, pool and synchronization delays as well as execution samples.
designGuide.cost: Profiles consume sampling overhead and need matching binaries, source revisions and a representative workload.

title: Build concurrency also has a memory budget
objective: Separate compiler work, runtime goroutines and caches when CI or a small machine stalls.
introduction: A burst of parallel compilation can exhaust memory before the program you are testing even starts. Build-cache misses, many packages, cgo and simultaneous jobs change the working set. Read the exact failing phase instead of assuming every slowdown is a goroutine scheduling issue in application code.

sections.title: Observe rather than clear every cache
sections.body: GOCACHE stores build artifacts while GOMODCACHE stores downloaded modules; these are different resources. A cache hit is useful only when the input and target match. Clearing both as the first troubleshooting step can amplify an outage by forcing every job to fetch and compile again.
sections.code:
go env GOCACHE GOMODCACHE
go build -x -p=2 ./...
go test -p=2 ./...
sections.walkthrough: The -x output reveals invoked tools and selected work. -p bounds build/test package parallelism, making it useful on constrained CI workers; it is separate from the deployed application’s connection and goroutine limits.

sections.title: Identify the runtime and the artifact
sections.body: Record the toolchain, module graph, target and build flags with the binary. go version -m inspects embedded build information. Repeat a clean dependency preparation in a fresh worktree or CI job when reproducibility is the question, instead of removing shared caches that other builds are using.
sections.code:
go version
go env GOOS GOARCH CGO_ENABLED
go build -trimpath -o ./bin/app ./cmd/app
go version -m ./bin/app
sections.walkthrough: The example assumes a real cmd/app package in your checkout. -trimpath removes certain local path information; it is not a substitute for pinning inputs or proving that two independently built artifacts have identical bytes.

sections.title: Set budgets at the correct layer
sections.body: A container memory limit, runtime GOMEMLIMIT, compiler package parallelism and application concurrency solve different problems. GOMEMLIMIT is a soft runtime target and does not cap all process or kernel memory. Change the limit indicated by evidence; increasing all limits can move the failure to the host.

takeaway: Locate the failing phase and its resource owner. Bound build jobs separately from runtime work, and retain caches and build provenance deliberately.
reviewAnswer: Bounds concurrent package work, not request goroutines
question: What does lowering go build -p primarily control?
wrongAnswers: The maximum number of HTTP requests in the built app
The database connection pool inside every package
hint: The build process and the deployed service have separate budgets.
nuance: The -p build flag limits concurrent package work in the toolchain. It does not impose a request, goroutine or database-connection limit on the compiled application.

strengths: Separate compiler work, runtime goroutines and caches when CI or a small machine stalls.
cautions: The -p build flag limits concurrent package work in the toolchain. It does not impose a request, goroutine or database-connection limit on the compiled application.
designGuide.cost: Lower package concurrency can increase build time while preventing memory exhaustion on a small worker.

title: Pin the compiler and the tools that generate your code
objective: Distinguish application dependencies, development commands and toolchain selection.
introduction: The binary that formats, generates or analyzes your project is part of the workflow’s input. An unpinned command on PATH can silently change generated output or lint results. Keep the intended tool version and compiler selection explicit without confusing them with the libraries your application imports.

sections.title: Read both go and toolchain directives
sections.body: The go directive states a module’s minimum Go version; a toolchain directive can suggest a toolchain for work on the main module. Depending on GOTOOLCHAIN, the go command may select or download another toolchain. CI should record its effective version instead of assuming PATH alone settles it.
sections.code:
go version
go env GOTOOLCHAIN GOMOD GOWORK
go mod edit -json
sections.walkthrough: Inspect the active module and its directives together. In a restricted or offline environment, automatic toolchain downloads may not be available; prepare the required supported compiler before the build.

sections.title: Install one reviewed command version
sections.body: A versioned go install command builds the selected command independently of the current module’s application dependencies. Newer Go versions also support tracking tools in go.mod; use the mechanism supported by your project toolchain and keep CI invocation consistent.
sections.code:
go install golang.org/x/vuln/cmd/govulncheck@v1.1.4
# Run the installed command from the configured GOBIN/PATH.
govulncheck ./...
sections.walkthrough: The version is an illustrative pin, not a claim that it is the latest release. Review and update tool pins deliberately; pinning avoids surprise changes but does not make an old tool permanently appropriate.

sections.title: Generators need the same discipline
sections.body: Document which generated outputs belong in version control and which are produced during a clean build. Test the generated delta and avoid a generator that relies on an uncommitted local replacement. Tool updates deserve a separate diff so semantic application changes remain reviewable.

takeaway: Record the effective compiler and reviewed tool versions. Keep generation reproducible and separate from ordinary library-version selection.
reviewAnswer: Makes a command version explicit, not permanently safe
question: Why pin development commands used by CI?
wrongAnswers: To make every future security update unnecessary
To force all application libraries to the same version number
hint: Reproducibility and ongoing maintenance both matter.
nuance: A reviewed tool pin makes CI’s command input reproducible. It still needs maintenance; it neither fixes all dependencies to one version nor removes future security work.

strengths: Distinguish application dependencies, development commands and toolchain selection.
cautions: A reviewed tool pin makes CI’s command input reproducible. It still needs maintenance; it neither fixes all dependencies to one version nor removes future security work.
designGuide.cost: Pinned tools and compilers make output reproducible but add an explicit dependency-update responsibility.

title: Test unknown inputs and check reachable vulnerabilities
objective: Combine fuzzing, regression seeds and govulncheck without treating one green tool as complete assurance.
introduction: Normal tests often cover the examples you already understand. Parsers and protocol boundaries also receive truncated, oversized and surprising inputs. Fuzzing explores input behavior, while vulnerability analysis asks whether known vulnerable code is reachable; the two tools answer different questions.

sections.title: Choose a property with a real oracle
sections.body: A useful fuzz property can check round trips, bounded output, valid parsing or equivalent behavior between implementations. Avoid a property that merely repeats the implementation. Bound input size and work so one accidental huge allocation does not consume the entire test budget.
sections.walkthrough: The fragment imports testing and strconv and asserts a defined parse/format/parse round trip for accepted integers. Rejected strings are allowed by the parser contract. For your own parser, choose an equally explicit invariant and retain meaningful failures as regression seeds.

sections.title: Give exploration and regression separate jobs
sections.body: Run a bounded fuzz campaign in a development environment and commit the small failing seed that explains a fixed bug. Ordinary go test reruns seed corpus inputs without launching an open-ended fuzz search. Vulnerability checks should use a reviewed current database and tool in connected CI.
sections.code:
go test ./internal/parser -fuzz=FuzzIntegerRoundTrip -fuzztime=20s
go test ./...
govulncheck ./...
sections.walkthrough: The package path is illustrative and must contain the target. Fuzz time bounds the campaign; source-level vulnerability findings still need interpretation against the built artifact, call path and deployment configuration.

sections.title: Keep the conclusion proportional to the evidence
sections.body: A green scan only reports what the analyzer and its current vulnerability database know. It does not inspect every operational configuration or prove the absence of new vulnerabilities. A clean fuzz run means the explored inputs did not violate the asserted properties within that budget.

takeaway: Use a meaningful bounded input property, retain regression seeds and analyze dependency findings in context. No single tool replaces behavior and deployment review.
reviewAnswer: Report bounded evidence, not absence of every bug
question: What does a passing bounded fuzz run establish?
wrongAnswers: All possible inputs have been exhaustively checked
Dependency security no longer needs maintenance
hint: State the input budget and the property actually asserted.
nuance: A weak property can pass even when the parser is wrong; choose an oracle tied to the contract.

strengths: Combine fuzzing, regression seeds and govulncheck without treating one green tool as complete assurance.
cautions: A weak property can pass even when the parser is wrong; choose an oracle tied to the contract.
designGuide.cost: Fuzzing spends a bounded compute budget; vulnerability findings require a maintained database and a reachable-code interpretation.

title: Package initialization is not a request-time connection factory
objective: Move fallible setup to an explicit owner and close shared resources after work drains.
introduction: Imported packages initialize before main, and hidden setup can turn an import into a database connection, network wait or process-wide configuration decision. Make those dependencies visible at the composition root so startup, tests, retries and shutdown share a clear owner.

sections.title: Keep fallible startup explicit
sections.body: A constructor can return an error and accept a caller-owned context; init cannot return an error to its caller. Build shared clients once, check readiness with a bounded operation, and inject them into handlers. Do not construct a new pool every time a request arrives.
sections.walkthrough: This is an application-structure fragment: loadConfig, openStore and serve belong to the application. The ordering exposes error propagation and ownership, while real shutdown must let active handlers finish before the shared store closes.

sections.title: Audit hidden work in dependencies
sections.body: Look for init functions, package-level constructors, mutable registries and side-effect imports. Some registration is intentional; expensive or fallible runtime work needs a visible reason. An import cycle is a package-graph problem, not a request concurrency problem.
sections.code:
go list -deps ./cmd/app
go list -f '{{.ImportPath}}: {{.Imports}}' ./internal/...
go test -count=1 ./...
sections.walkthrough: The commands show dependency paths and exercise a fresh test run. They do not inspect hidden effects automatically; combine the graph with reading constructors and initialization code at the boundaries you own.

sections.title: Budget readiness and shutdown
sections.body: A readiness check should answer whether this instance can serve useful work, not hammer every dependency on every health probe. Stop new work, drain in-flight requests within a deadline, then close shared clients. Use a new bounded cleanup context when the request context is already canceled.

takeaway: Give fallible setup, request work and cleanup explicit owners. Reuse shared clients, preserve deadlines and test startup failure and shutdown ordering.
reviewAnswer: Construct once; close after owned work drains
question: Who should own a service-wide database client?
wrongAnswers: Each handler creates and forgets its own pool
Every imported package silently creates one in init
hint: Match resource lifetime to the component that uses it.
nuance: The application component owns a shared client across requests, stops new work and drains existing work before closing it. Per-request pools multiply connection and startup costs.

strengths: Move fallible setup to an explicit owner and close shared resources after work drains.
cautions: The application component owns a shared client across requests, stops new work and drains existing work before closing it. Per-request pools multiply connection and startup costs.
designGuide.cost: Explicit startup and drain ordering take code, but make connection ownership, failure and tests observable.

title: MongoDB: one client, explicit deadlines and typed documents
objective: Connect with the Go v2 driver and separate construction, readiness, request work and cleanup.
introduction: MongoDB stores BSON documents and the Go driver manages discovery and pools for the deployment. A collection handle is not a new physical connection. Reuse a client across requests, model the fields the application owns, and keep network setup outside request-time package initialization.

sections.title: Construct the client and probe readiness
sections.body: The example uses go.mongodb.org/mongo-driver/v2, with v2.3.1 as a reproducible example pin. Connect constructs the client; a successful Ping is separate evidence that a server is reachable. In a native development checkout, obtain the URI from configuration and use the deployment’s required authentication and TLS.
sections.code:
client, err := mongo.Connect(options.Client().ApplyURI(uri).SetMaxPoolSize(16))
if err != nil { return err }
probe, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 2*time.Second)
err = client.Ping(probe, readpref.Primary())
cancel()
if err != nil {
    cleanup, stop := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), time.Second)
    defer stop()
    _ = client.Disconnect(cleanup)
    return err
}
sections.walkthrough: The fragment belongs to a startup function returning error and imports context, time, mongo, mongo/options and mongo/readpref from the v2 driver. The pool size is illustrative, not a production sizing recommendation.

sections.title: Decode into a deliberate schema
sections.body: Use BSON tags and explicit field types instead of letting every layer pass an unstructured map. Validate external input before constructing a query. ErrNoDocuments is an expected absence case when the contract allows it; it is different from a timeout, authorization failure or decode error.
sections.walkthrough: notes is a collection from the shared client; tenant and id come from validated application inputs. The application defines ErrNotFound. An omitted tenant predicate could become a data-isolation bug even if the database query is fast.

sections.title: Use separate lifetimes
sections.body: Every request operation should inherit a bounded caller context. Startup probes and final Disconnect need their own lifetimes; do not reuse an already canceled request context for cleanup. These native service snippets are reading material: GopherForge does not add remote MongoDB sockets to its WASI execution sandbox.

takeaway: Reuse a configured v2 client, prove readiness separately, decode explicit BSON models and distinguish absence from infrastructure failures.
reviewAnswer: Does not alone prove server readiness
question: What does a successful mongo.Connect call establish?
wrongAnswers: Every future operation will complete within its deadline
A new client must be created for each collection operation
hint: Construction and a bounded server operation are separate events.
nuance: Connect configures a client; a bounded Ping separately tests current server readiness. Neither promises that future network operations cannot fail or time out.

strengths: Connect with the Go v2 driver and separate construction, readiness, request work and cleanup.
cautions: Connect configures a client; a bounded Ping separately tests current server readiness. Neither promises that future network operations cannot fail or time out.
designGuide.cost: One shared client owns pools and topology monitoring; each additional service instance multiplies that connection demand.

title: MongoDB: design the query and its compound index together
objective: Use explain evidence, tenant predicates and stable pagination rather than adding indexes blindly.
introduction: A query that is fast with ten documents may scan a large collection after real traffic arrives. Shape the filter, sort and returned fields around an actual use case, then inspect the execution plan and the documents examined. Indexes improve selected reads while adding write, memory and maintenance cost.

sections.title: Create an index for one access pattern
sections.body: In an isolated development database, consider a tenant’s newest notes. A compound index starts with tenant equality and then the chosen sort keys. Keep the tie-breaker consistent with pagination so equal timestamps do not create unstable page boundaries.
sections.code:
db.notes.createIndex({tenant: 1, createdAt: -1, _id: -1})
db.notes.find({tenant: "demo"}, {body: 1, createdAt: 1})
  .sort({createdAt: -1, _id: -1}).limit(20).explain("executionStats")
sections.walkthrough: These mongosh commands assume demo documents in a development database. Compare nReturned, totalKeysExamined and totalDocsExamined and inspect the winning plan; explain executionStats runs the query and can itself add load.

sections.title: Use a stable continuation predicate
sections.body: For descending pagination, continue before the last (createdAt, _id) pair instead of repeatedly skipping an ever-growing number of earlier results. Match the sort and predicate with the index, and define what happens when documents change between pages.
sections.walkthrough: The timestamp and ObjectId are example continuation values, not an offset. New writes may change a live listing; a stable ordering is not automatically a snapshot of the collection across multiple requests.

sections.title: Verify selectivity and write cost
sections.body: A large limit, broad regex, missing tenant condition or incompatible sort can overwhelm a previously adequate pool. Index order, multikey behavior and collation affect usable plans. Measure representative data distribution and write latency before retaining another index; hints can hide a modeling error.

takeaway: Design filter, sort, projection and continuation together, verify examined work with explain, and account for index maintenance on every write.
reviewAnswer: Trades selected read work for storage and write cost
question: Why inspect explain after creating an index?
wrongAnswers: Any index guarantees constant-time queries
Pool size determines whether every query uses its index
hint: Compare work examined with useful rows returned.
nuance: The useful plan depends on filter, sort, selectivity and index shape. Explain measures examined work; a client pool setting does not guarantee index use.

strengths: Use explain evidence, tenant predicates and stable pagination rather than adding indexes blindly.
cautions: The useful plan depends on filter, sort, selectivity and index shape. Explain measures examined work; a client pool setting does not guarantee index use.
designGuide.cost: Each index consumes storage, memory and write maintenance; keep it only when the measured access pattern earns that cost.

title: MongoDB: put the invariant in the write predicate
objective: Prevent lost updates with atomic operators and optimistic version checks.
introduction: Reading a document, changing a field in Go and writing it back leaves a window for another request to change the same value. Memory race detection cannot find that distributed lost update. Express the allowed transition in the database predicate and inspect whether the write actually matched.

sections.title: Update fields without replacing unrelated state
sections.body: Use an atomic field operator when it expresses the intended operation. A client-side read followed by replacement can lose a concurrent edit or erase fields the caller never loaded. Include ownership predicates such as the tenant in the write, not only in the earlier read.
sections.walkthrough: This fragment assumes the shared v2 driver collection and application variables. A zero match can mean stale version or absence; map that to the application contract rather than reporting an unconditional successful save.

sections.title: Enforce uniqueness where concurrent writers meet
sections.body: A preliminary find cannot guarantee that another request will not insert the same business key. Define a unique index for that invariant and handle duplicate-key errors deliberately. In multi-tenant systems, decide whether uniqueness is global or scoped to a tenant.
sections.walkthrough: The example is a development upsert keyed by a stable external identifier. Review existing duplicate data before adding the unique index; deployment of an invariant is itself a migration that can fail.

sections.title: Single-document atomicity has a boundary
sections.body: One atomic update does not make a two-document business operation atomic. Prefer a document model that contains the invariant when practical, or use a transaction with a clear cost and retry policy. Avoid promising exactly-once business effects just because the driver can retry an eligible write.

takeaway: Use conditional atomic writes and database-enforced uniqueness for concurrent invariants. Treat unmatched writes and duplicate keys as meaningful outcomes.
reviewAnswer: Is an outcome to handle, not automatic success
question: What must a version-checked update inspect after no driver error?
wrongAnswers: Only whether the preceding read found a document
Whether the Go race detector reported shared memory
hint: No driver error does not imply that the predicate matched.
nuance: No driver error does not mean the predicate matched. Check MatchedCount and handle an absent or stale-version document; one-document atomicity does not cover every business invariant.

strengths: Prevent lost updates with atomic operators and optimistic version checks.
cautions: No driver error does not mean the predicate matched. Check MatchedCount and handle an absent or stale-version document; one-document atomicity does not cover every business invariant.
designGuide.cost: Version conflicts become visible application outcomes; the caller needs retry, merge or user-facing conflict behavior.

title: MongoDB transactions: retry database work, not external effects
objective: Choose transaction boundaries, concerns and idempotency for ambiguous failures.
introduction: A transaction can protect a multi-document invariant, but it adds coordination and can retry work. A callback that charges a card or sends email while updating documents can repeat an external effect. Keep the database transition inside the transaction and move external delivery behind an explicit durable boundary.

sections.title: Keep session work sequential and owned
sections.body: The Go v2 driver’s WithTransaction callback receives the context that operations in the transaction must use. Do not share a session concurrently across goroutines or start parallel operations inside one transaction. A replica-set or supported sharded deployment is required; a standalone local server is not equivalent.
sections.walkthrough: The application constructs order and event with stable operation identifiers and uses collections from the same shared client. The callback contains database work only; the outbox consumer sends the external notification after commit.

sections.title: Define what committed means for this operation
sections.body: Read concern, write concern and read preference affect visibility and acknowledgment. A timeout or lost response can leave the caller unsure whether a commit happened. Reconcile using the durable operation ID rather than assuming every error means nothing changed.
sections.code:
db.orders.createIndex({operationID: 1}, {unique: true})
db.outbox.createIndex({eventID: 1}, {unique: true})
db.orders.findOne({operationID: "checkout-demo-42"})
sections.walkthrough: These development commands illustrate the durable keys used for reconciliation. Unique identifiers do not on their own deliver an external effect exactly once; the receiver and delivery process also need idempotency.

sections.title: Test the failure windows
sections.body: Inject a transient transaction failure, an ambiguous commit response and a consumer crash after sending but before marking delivery. Verify the resulting invariant and duplicate handling. Short transactions reduce contention; do not perform slow HTTP calls or user interaction while holding a transaction open.

takeaway: A retryable transaction callback should contain repeatable database work. Use durable operation IDs and an outbox when the business action crosses systems.
reviewAnswer: Can repeat its application-side code
question: Why keep an external payment call outside WithTransaction?
wrongAnswers: MongoDB automatically rolls back every remote HTTP service
A shared session makes all goroutines globally sequential
hint: The database cannot undo an effect in another system.
nuance: The driver can rerun the transaction callback. MongoDB cannot roll back an external payment or email, so make database work repeatable and deliver external effects through an idempotent boundary.

strengths: Choose transaction boundaries, concerns and idempotency for ambiguous failures.
cautions: The driver can rerun the transaction callback. MongoDB cannot roll back an external payment or email, so make database work repeatable and deliver external effects through an idempotent boundary.
designGuide.cost: Transactions add coordination and contention; the outbox adds durable records, delivery workers and duplicate handling.

title: MongoDB cursors: bound the result and close the stream
objective: Avoid loading an unbounded collection into application memory.
introduction: A cursor lets an application consume a result in batches; it is not permission to read the entire database without a budget. The query, projection, batch size, total limit and request deadline jointly determine network work and application memory. Check errors after iteration, not only when opening the cursor.

sections.title: Iterate with a deadline and a total limit
sections.body: The v2 cursor’s Next can fail after some documents have already been decoded. Close the cursor on every path and propagate decode and cursor errors. A batch size controls transfer grouping; a total limit controls how much useful work the request is willing to perform.
sections.walkthrough: The fragment assumes a bounded ctx, the application’s Note model and a consumer that does not retain every document. Cleanup gets a fresh bounded context so a canceled request does not prevent the cursor-close attempt.

sections.title: Project only what this path needs
sections.body: For a list view, return a small subset rather than large embedded payloads. Calling All on an unbounded cursor can materialize the whole result and exhaust memory. BatchSize does not impose a total row limit or protect you if consume appends every document to a slice.
sections.code:
db.notes.find({tenant: "demo"}, {body: 1, createdAt: 1})
  .sort({createdAt: -1, _id: -1}).limit(100).batchSize(25)
sections.walkthrough: The development shell query caps the result independently of the batch size. Keep a supporting index for the actual filter and sort and measure response bytes as well as document count.

sections.title: Own downstream backpressure
sections.body: If documents are sent to worker goroutines, use a bounded channel and cancellation path. Otherwise a streaming query can simply move the unbounded queue into Go memory. Do not concurrently use one cursor from multiple goroutines; give iteration one owner and distribute decoded values deliberately.

takeaway: Bound total work separately from batch grouping, inspect cursor.Err, close on every path, and keep downstream buffering bounded.
reviewAnswer: Controls batches, not the total result limit
question: Why is a small batch size insufficient protection against memory growth?
wrongAnswers: It makes the server ignore all query predicates
It automatically discards every decoded document
hint: The consumer may still retain every batch.
nuance: Streaming only stays memory-bounded when the query and downstream consumer both have explicit limits.

strengths: Avoid loading an unbounded collection into application memory.
cautions: Streaming only stays memory-bounded when the query and downstream consumer both have explicit limits.
designGuide.cost: Bounded iteration reduces retained memory but requires cursor ownership, cancellation and downstream backpressure.

title: MongoDB under load: budget waiting before enlarging the pool
objective: Separate server selection, pool checkout, query time and application queueing.
introduction: When every operation slows down, a larger pool can multiply pressure on the same database. Investigate where the deadline is spent: waiting in the application, selecting a server, checking out a connection, creating a socket or executing a query. Count all application instances and topology servers in the capacity model.

sections.title: Reuse a bounded shared client
sections.body: A pool is associated with a server in the topology; monitoring connections add to the total. MaxPoolSize limits active pool capacity, not the number of goroutines allowed to wait. Give operations a deadline and bound application admission so overload does not become an invisible growing queue.
sections.code:
opts := options.Client().ApplyURI(uri).
    SetMaxPoolSize(16).SetMaxConnecting(2).
    SetMaxConnIdleTime(60*time.Second).SetTimeout(2*time.Second)
client, err := mongo.Connect(opts)
if err != nil { return err }
sections.walkthrough: These are illustrative v2 settings for a small service, not universal recommendations. Estimate total connections across all instances and topology members and compare checkout wait with query duration before changing the cap.

sections.title: Use evidence from both client and database
sections.body: In a development environment, inspect operation behavior with an explain plan and server metrics. Add client-side pool and command monitoring at the application boundary; avoid logging credentials, raw documents or sensitive filter values in telemetry.
sections.code:
db.notes.find({tenant: "demo"}).limit(20).explain("executionStats")
db.serverStatus().connections
db.serverStatus().opcounters
sections.walkthrough: Availability of server metrics depends on deployment permissions and product. Correlate a time window of pool checkout wait, request errors and examined documents; a lifetime counter alone cannot explain current tail latency.

sections.title: Recover without a retry storm
sections.body: One overall deadline should cover queueing and attempts. Restrict retryable work and test server failover, pool saturation and slow-query recovery. Separate a deliberately slow bulk operation from latency-sensitive traffic when their budgets differ, and prefer fixing an inefficient query to adding thousands of waiting goroutines.

takeaway: Bound admission and waiting as well as sockets, then tune using correlated request, pool and query evidence. More connections do not repair an overloaded database.
reviewAnswer: Can increase pressure without reducing the bottleneck
question: What should precede a pool-size increase during high latency?
wrongAnswers: Adding an unbounded goroutine for every queued operation
Retrying every failed write forever
hint: Find the stage that consumes the operation deadline.
nuance: Client pool capacity, waiting goroutines and total deployment connections are different quantities.

strengths: Separate server selection, pool checkout, query time and application queueing.
cautions: Client pool capacity, waiting goroutines and total deployment connections are different quantities.
designGuide.cost: Admission limits trade immediate overload rejection for bounded waiting; tuning requires client and server telemetry together.

title: Redis: share the client and distinguish a miss from an outage
objective: Configure go-redis deadlines, connection budgets and explicit cache-miss behavior.
introduction: Redis is often used as a low-latency data-structure service, but the network, client pool and command cost still exist. Create a shared client, keep a bounded operation context and distinguish redis.Nil from transport failures. A missing optional cache entry and an unavailable required store have different application contracts.

sections.title: Construct one client with explicit example budgets
sections.body: This lesson uses github.com/redis/go-redis/v9 with v9.16.0 as an example pin. PoolSize and MaxActiveConns are distinct knobs; do not assume a pool’s preferred retained size is a universal hard ceiling. Confirm options against the pinned version rather than copying future-version defaults.
sections.walkthrough: The values illustrate a bounded small-client configuration, with automatic retries disabled so policy is visible. Production TLS, authentication and addresses come from configuration; re-enable suitable retries only with an overall operation budget and duplicate-effect analysis.

sections.title: Handle absence explicitly
sections.body: redis.Nil represents a missing key for a GET, not a dead server. Preserve other errors so a caller can apply the intended fallback or failure policy. A fallback that recomputes expensive data on every transport failure can overwhelm the primary database during a Redis outage.
sections.walkthrough: This is a helper returning string and error. The application supplies a bounded ctx and loadFromOrigin; the example deliberately surfaces infrastructure failure instead of silently starting unlimited origin requests.

sections.title: Keep version and workload assumptions visible
sections.body: Later client versions can change pooling and pipeline behavior. Pin and test the version used by the service, including cancellation and saturation. These native network examples are not executable Redis access inside the app’s WASI sandbox; they teach the surrounding Go service environment.

takeaway: Reuse the client, configure bounded waiting and handle value, miss and outage separately. Fallback and retry behavior are application decisions, not invisible conveniences.
reviewAnswer: Means the key is absent, not a connection outage
question: How should a GET cache miss differ from a transport error?
wrongAnswers: Treat both as evidence that Redis lost every key
Assume both guarantee an origin database request will be cheap
hint: Choose behavior for each error class.
nuance: redis.Nil from GET means this key is absent. A transport failure is a different result; unlimited fallback work during an outage can overwhelm the origin.

strengths: Configure go-redis deadlines, connection budgets and explicit cache-miss behavior.
cautions: redis.Nil from GET means this key is absent. A transport failure is a different result; unlimited fallback work during an outage can overwhelm the origin.
designGuide.cost: Shared pools save connection setup; their total size, retries and waiting must fit the deployment’s capacity budget.

title: Redis cache-aside: TTLs do not solve concurrent fills
objective: Design expiry, invalidation, negative caching and stampede control deliberately.
introduction: A cache duplicates another source of truth, so freshness and ownership must be explicit. Cache-aside reads can miss together, all query the origin and then repopulate the same key. TTL bounds one kind of staleness; it does not prevent a stampede or make a read-modify-write sequence correct.

sections.title: Set value and expiration together
sections.body: Use one SET operation with expiry when creating an expiring value. A separate SET followed by EXPIRE leaves a failure window where the key can survive without the intended lifetime. An ordinary later SET can also change existing TTL behavior, so decide the overwrite policy.
sections.code:
redis-cli SET demo:product:42 '{"name":"tea"}' EX 60
redis-cli GET demo:product:42
redis-cli TTL demo:product:42
sections.walkthrough: Run against an isolated development Redis using the demo namespace. TTL reports remaining expiry state, not freshness relative to a database update that happened after the value was cached.

sections.title: Bound concurrent misses
sections.body: Coalesce identical in-process fills and independently bound the total number of origin calls. A per-key singleflight group only coordinates callers in this process; many service replicas can still miss together. Optional TTL jitter spreads expirations but does not guarantee a global rate limit.
sections.walkthrough: The fragment shows the atomic value-plus-expiry client operation after an origin load. It does not implement coalescing or cross-process coordination; those policies belong to the loader boundary and must be tested separately.

sections.title: Handle stale and missing data as distinct cases
sections.body: Negative caching can reduce repeated absent-item lookups, but use a short deliberate lifetime and a representation distinct from a real value. A database update followed by cache deletion can race with an older in-flight fill. Use versioned keys or another coherent invalidation design when that stale-write window is unacceptable.

takeaway: Set TTL atomically, bound origin fills and define the acceptable stale window. TTL, coalescing and invalidation address different failure modes.
reviewAnswer: Does not prevent misses from flooding the origin
question: What extra protection does a cache-aside loader need during a burst of misses?
wrongAnswers: Only a longer TTL on keys that have not been created yet
One unlimited goroutine for every origin request
hint: Consider the empty-cache path, including all replicas.
nuance: In-process coalescing does not coordinate other replicas or make invalidation races disappear.

strengths: Design expiry, invalidation, negative caching and stampede control deliberately.
cautions: In-process coalescing does not coordinate other replicas or make invalidation races disappear.
designGuide.cost: Caching adds duplicate state, invalidation and miss coordination; measure saved origin work against stale-data risk.

title: Redis pipelines save round trips; they are not transactions
objective: Bound command batches, inspect command errors and separate batching from atomicity.
introduction: Pipelining lets a client send multiple commands without waiting for every individual round trip. It can improve throughput for independent work, but it does not make the group indivisible. Large batches also retain commands and replies in memory and can worsen latency for other work.

sections.title: Batch independent work
sections.body: Queue a small known batch and inspect the returned command objects. An error from Exec needs interpretation alongside each command result. A connection failure can leave the caller uncertain which writes the server executed; a batch is not an automatic rollback boundary.
sections.walkthrough: This fragment batches two independent reads and tolerates missing keys explicitly. A write pipeline needs its own partial-outcome and retry policy; replaying all writes after an ambiguous error can duplicate effects.

sections.title: Choose atomicity separately
sections.body: MULTI/EXEC groups commands atomically with respect to interleaving, but runtime command errors do not provide relational-database rollback. WATCH adds optimistic checks and can require a whole retry. A Lua script can perform a short conditional transition, but expensive scripts block other work on the server execution path.
sections.code:
redis-cli <<'REDIS'
MULTI
SET demo:a 1
INCR demo:count
EXEC
REDIS
sections.walkthrough: The heredoc sends all commands through one redis-cli connection against an isolated development instance. Starting separate redis-cli processes for MULTI and EXEC would not create one transaction; connection ownership is part of the protocol.

sections.title: Set a memory and latency budget for batches
sections.body: Cap commands and total encoded bytes, not only the number of business items. Measure batch duration, reply sizes and tail latency while other clients work. Client versions may use separate pipeline pools, so inspect the pinned version when calculating deployment-wide connection limits.

takeaway: Batch bounded independent work to reduce round trips, and choose atomicity and retry semantics explicitly. Inspect partial outcomes rather than assuming Exec implies rollback.
reviewAnswer: Batches round trips without making the group atomic
question: What does pipelining guarantee about the whole batch?
wrongAnswers: Every earlier write rolls back if a later command errors
No other client can execute a command between its commands
hint: Transport batching and a transactional boundary are different.
nuance: MULTI/EXEC does not roll back already executed commands after a runtime command error.

strengths: Bound command batches, inspect command errors and separate batching from atomicity.
cautions: MULTI/EXEC does not roll back already executed commands after a runtime command error.
designGuide.cost: Batches reduce network round trips while retaining command/reply memory and increasing ambiguous partial-outcome work.

title: Redis counters and leases need atomic transitions and ownership
objective: Avoid split increment/expiry races and unsafe lock deletion.
introduction: A counter with a timeout and a temporary ownership key look small, but concurrent requests and pauses expose their failure windows. Put dependent steps in one short atomic transition and distinguish an expired lease from a durable guarantee that only one worker can ever act.

sections.title: Make a fixed-window counter transition atomic
sections.body: INCR followed by EXPIRE in separate operations can leave a counter without expiry if the client fails between them. A short script can attach expiry only when the counter is first created. This is an anchored fixed-window example, not a smooth sliding-window limiter.
sections.code:
counter := redis.NewScript(`
local n = redis.call("INCR", KEYS[1])
if n == 1 then redis.call("PEXPIRE", KEYS[1], ARGV[1]) end
return n
`)
n, err := counter.Run(ctx, rdb, []string{"demo:rate"}, 1000).Int64()
if err != nil { return err }
if n > 100 { return ErrLimited }
sections.walkthrough: The go-redis script API passes one explicitly named development key and a positive window in milliseconds. This example permits 100 events in a window anchored at the first increment; ErrLimited is an application error. Define unavailable-store behavior separately.

sections.title: A lease must be released only by its owner
sections.body: SET key token NX PX can create a temporary lease. Release by checking the stored token and deleting in the same atomic operation, not by a GET and later DEL. Generate a unique token for each acquisition; a stale owner must not remove a new owner’s lease.
sections.code:
release := redis.NewScript(`
local current = redis.call("GET", KEYS[1])
if current == ARGV[1] then
  return redis.call("DEL", KEYS[1])
end
return 0
`)
// token is unique to this successful SET key token NX PX acquisition.
deleted, err := release.Run(ctx, rdb, []string{key}, token).Int64()
if err != nil { return err }
_ = deleted // 0 means the lease no longer belongs to this acquisition.
sections.walkthrough: The script compares the acquisition token inside the server before deletion. It solves that release race, but a paused worker may still continue after its lease expires; a protected resource may need fencing or another stronger ownership mechanism.

sections.title: Explain the failure model before calling it a lock
sections.body: An acknowledgment can be lost, a lease can expire during a pause and failover can change which writes survive. A Redis key alone is not a proof of exclusive business execution across failures. Use resource-side idempotency, version checks or fencing when duplicate work could violate an invariant.

takeaway: Make dependent counter steps atomic and release leases by token. Design the downstream invariant for pauses, ambiguity and expired ownership.
reviewAnswer: Does not stop a paused former owner from continuing
question: Why can a resource still need fencing after a lease expires?
wrongAnswers: Redis pauses every process that previously held the key
A unique token prevents all network failures
hint: A key’s lifetime and a process’s execution lifetime differ.
nuance: Expiry changes the Redis key, not the execution state of an old process. A paused former owner can resume after a new owner starts; the protected resource may need fencing.

strengths: Avoid split increment/expiry races and unsafe lock deletion.
cautions: Expiry changes the Redis key, not the execution state of an old process. A paused former owner can resume after a new owner starts; the protected resource may need fencing.
designGuide.cost: Atomic scripts add protocol and recovery complexity; a lease is weaker than a durable resource-side ownership guarantee.

title: Redis Streams: acknowledge after the durable effect
objective: Understand consumer groups, pending entries, redelivery and bounded retention.
introduction: A consumer group tracks delivery and acknowledgment, not automatic exactly-once application effects. A worker may crash after updating another database but before XACK. Redelivery is useful recovery, so the handler must recognize an operation it has already applied.

sections.title: Read new entries with one group
sections.body: In an isolated development instance, create a stream and group and append a demonstration event. XREADGROUP with > asks for new entries for this group. Acknowledge only after the application’s durable effect succeeds.
sections.code:
redis-cli XGROUP CREATE demo:events workers 0 MKSTREAM
redis-cli XADD demo:events '*' operationID order-42 kind created
redis-cli XREADGROUP GROUP workers worker-1 COUNT 10 STREAMS demo:events '>'
sections.walkthrough: Replace worker names per process and retain the stream entry ID returned by the read. The demonstration group starts from 0 intentionally; starting at $ instead changes whether existing history is delivered.

sections.title: Inspect and reclaim pending entries
sections.body: A delivered but unacknowledged entry remains pending for the group. Inspect pending work and use a supported reclaim mechanism after an appropriate idle threshold. A slow healthy worker and a dead worker can look alike, so claiming work must not assume the old consumer has physically stopped.
sections.code:
redis-cli XPENDING demo:events workers
redis-cli XAUTOCLAIM demo:events workers worker-2 60000 0-0 COUNT 10
# After the effect succeeds, acknowledge its actual returned entry ID:
# redis-cli XACK demo:events workers 1710000000000-0
sections.walkthrough: XAUTOCLAIM requires a compatible server version and returns a continuation cursor as well as claimed entries. Iterate with explicit work bounds; the sample acknowledgment ID is a placeholder, not a success shortcut.

sections.title: Keep delivery, retention and durability distinct
sections.body: Deduplicate the operation at the durable destination and treat replay as a normal path. Configure stream trimming so it does not discard work that still matters to consumers. Acknowledgment does not itself specify Redis persistence, replication acknowledgment or recovery guarantees; test those separately for the deployment.

takeaway: Acknowledge after a durable idempotent effect, recover pending work deliberately, and budget retention and storage independently of consumer-group delivery.
reviewAnswer: Can cause redelivery after an effect already happened
question: Why must a stream consumer make its external effect idempotent?
wrongAnswers: Consumer groups roll back all external databases on failure
Reading with > guarantees an entry is delivered only once forever
hint: The worker can fail between the effect and acknowledgment.
nuance: The effect may commit before a worker crashes without acknowledging. Redelivery can then repeat it; pending-entry recovery needs destination-side idempotency.

strengths: Understand consumer groups, pending entries, redelivery and bounded retention.
cautions: The effect may commit before a worker crashes without acknowledging. Redelivery can then repeat it; pending-entry recovery needs destination-side idempotency.
designGuide.cost: Consumer groups need retention, pending-work recovery, idempotent effects and explicit storage durability.

title: Redis under load: hot keys, memory pressure and ambiguous retries
objective: Inspect server latency and memory while bounding client work and retry amplification.
introduction: Redis command latency can rise because of expensive commands, a hot key, big values, persistence work, network delay or waiting in the client. A low average hides queues and timeout bursts. Correlate request errors with server and client evidence before increasing goroutines or connection limits.

sections.title: Use focused observation commands
sections.body: In an authorized development environment, inspect memory, command statistics and recent slow commands. SLOWLOG measures server command execution, not every network or client-pool delay. Keep raw keys and command arguments out of broadly shared diagnostics when they may contain user data.
sections.code:
redis-cli INFO memory
redis-cli INFO stats
redis-cli INFO commandstats
redis-cli SLOWLOG GET 10
redis-cli LATENCY LATEST
sections.walkthrough: Metrics and latency monitoring availability depend on server configuration and permissions. Compare the same time window with client pool wait and request p99; a quiet SLOWLOG does not prove that callers were fast.

sections.title: Scan incrementally and cap batch work
sections.body: KEYS can block while traversing a large keyspace. SCAN divides that work into cursor-driven steps, but it is not a snapshot, COUNT is a hint and keys may appear more than once. Keep downstream handling idempotent and avoid moving all returned keys into one giant slice.
sections.code:
redis-cli SCAN 0 MATCH 'demo:*' COUNT 100
# Continue with the returned cursor until it is 0.
redis-cli MEMORY USAGE demo:product:42
sections.walkthrough: A single SCAN call is not a complete inventory. Even incremental maintenance needs rate and time budgets; do not run an unbounded sweep simply because each individual command looks small.

sections.title: Define storage and retry guarantees
sections.body: Eviction policy and persistence determine whether a value can disappear and what survives failure. Replication is not automatically synchronous durability. Retrying INCR after a lost response may apply the effect twice; use an operation identifier and a suitable atomic protocol when duplicate effects are unacceptable. Bound retries within one deadline and measure recovery after overload.

takeaway: Separate client wait from server execution, keep maintenance incremental and design for eviction, persistence and ambiguous write outcomes. More concurrency is not a repair for a hot bottleneck.
reviewAnswer: Does not exclude client-pool or network latency
question: Why can callers time out while SLOWLOG shows no slow commands?
wrongAnswers: Redis always measures the full HTTP request path
SCAN COUNT imposes an exact global rate limit
hint: Locate waiting before and after server command execution.
nuance: SLOWLOG measures server execution. Callers can still wait for a client connection or network response; retries can then amplify load or repeat an ambiguous write.

strengths: Inspect server latency and memory while bounding client work and retry amplification.
cautions: SLOWLOG measures server execution. Callers can still wait for a client connection or network response; retries can then amplify load or repeat an ambiguous write.
designGuide.cost: Latency and eviction policies trade memory, availability and persistence work; client concurrency cannot remove a hot-key bottleneck.

title: Borrow bytes briefly; copy before their owner changes
objective: Trace bytes.Buffer and Scanner views, then make retained results independent at a lifetime boundary.
introduction: A byte slice can be a borrowed window rather than an owned result. bytes.Buffer.Bytes exposes unread storage, and Scanner.Bytes exposes a token with a limited lifetime. The type []byte does not express that lifetime. Draw the owner, the view and the next mutation before deciding whether to copy.

sections.title: One owner, one temporary view
sections.body: Draw a row of bytes for the buffer, then a window labeled view above it. Bytes does not create a separate row. While the borrow is valid, changing an element through the view changes the buffer. A separate copy belongs on a second row with no shared storage.
sections.code:
package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "fmt"
)

func main() {
    var buffer bytes.Buffer
    buffer.WriteString("alpha")
    view := buffer.Bytes()
    owned := bytes.Clone(view)
    view[0] = 'A'
    fmt.Println(buffer.String())
    buffer.Reset()
    buffer.WriteString("omega")
    fmt.Println(string(owned))
}
sections.walkthrough: The output is Alpha, then alpha. The first print demonstrates aliasing before reset. bytes.Clone creates the owned result before the owner changes. The program deliberately never inspects view after reset: its old contents are not a valid result to rely on.

sections.title: The lifetime timeline
sections.body: Follow this order: obtain a view, consume it synchronously, then mutate or release the owner. If you must return, cache or enqueue the result beyond that boundary, copy the bytes or transfer the owner explicitly. Assigning the slice to another variable copies its descriptor and preserves sharing. Clip also keeps the existing elements shared.

sections.title: Scanner tokens need the same decision
sections.body: Scanner.Bytes may expose storage reused by the next Scan. A token consumed immediately can remain borrowed. A token saved in a collection needs its own bytes. Check Scanner.Err after the loop as a separate requirement; correct ownership does not make input parsing infallible.
sections.walkthrough: Each iteration copies the current token before the next Scan can replace it. The saved values therefore print red and blue. Without a copy, storing the slice descriptors would not establish a durable token contract. The final error check handles scanning failures independently.

sections.title: Asynchronous work crosses the boundary
sections.body: A successful channel send transfers the slice descriptor, not an immutable snapshot. The producer must stop using the storage until consumption finishes, or send an owned copy. For cancellation, specify who owns a buffer when enqueueing fails and who releases it after a successful handoff.

sections.title: Reset, retention and tests
sections.body: Reset prepares a buffer for reuse and can retain its allocation. It does not guarantee erasure of sensitive bytes. Test that an owned result remains unchanged after later buffer operations. Avoid tests that require a particular stale value from an invalid view, and measure retained memory when large buffers live much longer than their input.

takeaway: A borrowed result is safe only within its documented lifetime. Draw the next mutation or release, then copy before that boundary when the caller needs a durable value. Test independence of valid results rather than the contents of invalid views.
reviewAnswer: Copy before owner changes
question: A result must survive bytes.Buffer.Reset and later writes. What establishes independent ownership?
wrongAnswers: Clip the view to its length
Assign the slice to a new name
hint: A second descriptor still refers to the same backing array.
nuance: Clone copies the bytes. Reset does not revoke aliases or promise to overwrite old storage. A channel send also copies a descriptor, so asynchronous consumption needs an ownership protocol.

strengths: Borrow for immediate synchronous work
Copy only at a lifetime boundary
Document validity in the API
cautions: Clip does not copy
Sending a slice does not freeze it
Reset is not secret erasure
designGuide.cost: One deliberate copy buys independent result lifetime. Measure the boundary rather than guessing from allocation count.

title: A pool reuses temporary objects; it does not own your results
objective: Use sync.Pool with exclusive ownership, independent output and an explicit policy for oversized buffers.
introduction: Pooling can reduce temporary allocation, but every Get and Put creates an ownership obligation. A former owner must stop using the object after Put. A result that still aliases the object violates that obligation even when the code compiles and a small benchmark looks fast.

sections.title: Draw the ownership cycle
sections.body: Follow Get to one active owner, then produce an independent result before Put. After release, the old owner must not read or write the buffer. The pool can discard objects and Get need not return a previously stored object, so correctness must work with both reuse and a fresh allocation.

sections.title: Copy the result before releasing its storage
sections.body: This encoder returns owned bytes. Its example cutoff avoids deliberately returning an oversized backing buffer to this pool. The cutoff is a workload policy, not a universal value and not a cap on total process memory.
sections.walkthrough: The output remains hello, Ada after another encode. bytes.Clone separates the result from temporary storage before Put. The example never assumes the second call gets the same buffer. Buffers larger than the illustrative cutoff are discarded from this reuse path, while active requests and returned results still consume memory.

sections.title: Do not turn a pool into a resource budget
sections.body: sync.Pool is not a bounded cache, a reliable queue, or a database connection manager. Objects can disappear without explicit removal. A strict concurrency limit needs admission control; a database connection needs its client library's capacity, timeout and cleanup rules. A pool alone establishes none of those contracts.

sections.title: Test public independence, not object identity
sections.body: Keep the first result, make many later calls, and verify the first bytes remain unchanged. Add parallel calls under the race detector. Do not assert that a specific object returns from Get. Test large and small inputs, and check cancellation ownership if work is queued to another goroutine.

sections.title: Make the optimization earn its protocol
sections.body: Compare a correct unpooled baseline against the pooled version using realistic response-size distributions. Measure allocations, retained memory and latency after bursts. Race instrumentation is for correctness checks, not production timing claims. If pooling adds complexity without a measurable benefit, keep the simpler owned-result implementation.

takeaway: Get gives temporary exclusive access; Put ends it. Make external results independent before release, avoid identity assumptions and measure whether pooling helps. A per-object size cutoff does not bound total memory or concurrent work.
reviewAnswer: Copy before Put
question: A function returns a buffer to sync.Pool. How can its returned []byte remain safe for the caller?
wrongAnswers: Read it after Put if usually unchanged
Require Get to return the last object
hint: A later owner may reuse storage immediately; the returned value needs a separate lifetime.
nuance: Pool reuse is optional and identity is not guaranteed. An owned copy remains correct with or without reuse. A pool does not replace admission control, a bounded queue or database connection management.

strengths: Reuse measured temporary allocation
Keep the boundary in one small function
Correct with reuse or fresh allocation
cautions: No access after Put
No guaranteed object retention
No hard memory bound
designGuide.cost: Extra ownership protocol and possible retained capacity. Keep an unpooled baseline and discard oversized objects according to workload.

title: JSON v2: migrate behavior, not just imports
objective: Compare null, empty and omitted JSON values before changing a public API.
introduction: Go 1.27 includes encoding/json/v2 without an experiment flag. Keeping encoding/json preserves its v1 behavior; adopting the v2 API is a separate decision. A compiling change can still alter a mobile model, persisted event or generated client. Write the expected wire representation before migrating.

sections.title: Compare a zero-valued response
sections.body: Ordinary nil slices and maps become empty collections under v2 defaults. V1 produces null. Neither representation is universally better: an established client may distinguish absence from an empty result. Keep fixtures for the actual exported types, including binary data and custom methods.
sections.walkthrough: The two valid JSON documents carry different collection shapes. This complete program uses only the Go 1.27 standard library. The panic checks belong to a small demonstration; an application boundary should return and classify encoding errors.

sections.title: Preserve first, opt in deliberately
sections.body: DefaultOptionsV1 supplies the compatibility baseline through the v2 API. Later options override earlier ones, so opt into one reviewed change and keep the rest of the contract stable. A compatibility option does not validate domain data or automatically version persisted messages.
sections.walkthrough: This function-body fragment imports encoding/json as jsonv1, encoding/json/v2 as jsonv2, and fmt. response is the application value. Only nil-slice formatting is deliberately changed; nil-map behavior stays at the chosen v1 baseline.

sections.title: Test old readers as well as new writers
sections.body: Compare typed meaning and exact bytes separately. Sorted map output is useful for snapshots, but deterministic encoding is not a universal canonicalization format for signatures. Include old stored records, custom marshalers and independently released consumers, then stage the rollout with sampled comparisons and a format-aware rollback.

sections.title: Extend the exercise
sections.body: Keep an empty response fixture and a nonempty one. Change one option, predict the output, run both packages and explain which consumer needs the old result. The longer workshop on the website includes strict decoding, race-tested contract examples and a bounded fuzz target. It is useful preparation before a repository-wide import rewrite.

takeaway: Preserve the established JSON contract first. Enable an intentional representation change only when fixtures and consumers agree about its meaning.
reviewAnswer: Preserve, compare, then opt in
question: An existing endpoint must keep nil maps encoded as null during migration. Which approach fits?
wrongAnswers: Replace every import and trust the compiler
Make every field a string
hint: A new API surface and a new wire representation are separate changes.

title: JSON presence: omitted, zero and null are different states
objective: Choose omitempty, omitzero and request presence models from the endpoint contract.
introduction: A JSON object can omit a member, contain null, or contain a concrete zero value. Go fields alone do not always preserve those distinctions. An update that sets enabled to false must not silently become an instruction to leave enabled unchanged. Start with a state table for the operation.

sections.title: Compare omission rules
sections.body: Under v1 defaults, omitempty omits a zero integer and false boolean. Under v2 defaults those are nonempty JSON values and remain present. omitzero expresses Go zero-value omission. Do not replace tags mechanically: some response fields must be visible even when false or zero.
sections.walkthrough: These declarations compare ordinary scalar fields. They do not describe every custom marshaler. Build table tests for zero, nonzero, nil and explicitly empty values on the actual request or response type.

sections.title: Do not use an ordinary bool as a PATCH protocol

A *bool can distinguish absent from false in a freshly decoded value, but ordinary decoding also maps explicit null to nil. If null means clear while absence means keep, use a documented presence-aware representation or an explicit operation type.

sections.title: A complete update has a simpler contract
sections.body: For a full replacement command, decide required fields and validate the final state. For a partial update, separately validate which transitions are allowed. Avoid reusing an already populated decoding target: fields absent from input can retain earlier state and make missing values appear supplied.

sections.title: Write the four cases before the code
sections.body: Test an omitted property, null, false and true independently. Assert both the final stored value and whether a write occurs. Add unknown members and malformed values to the matrix, and verify that decoding or validation failure cannot publish a partial update.

takeaway: Specify presence semantics before choosing tags or pointer fields. Missing, null and a concrete zero value may represent different commands.

question: Ordinary decoding into a fresh *bool must distinguish missing, null and false. What is missing from that representation?
wrongAnswers: Pointers always distinguish all three states
omitempty validates required input
hint: Ask what a pointer contains after null and after an omitted property.

title: Strict JSON input: reject ambiguity before side effects
objective: Separate JSON syntax acceptance, unknown-member policy and domain validation.
introduction: Successful decoding proves only that input was accepted under the decoder policy. It does not authorize the caller or establish a valid business transition. V2 rejects duplicate names and invalid UTF-8 by default; exact field-name matching and unknown-member rejection are separate settings.

sections.title: Make the boundary policy visible
sections.body: Unknown members are ignored by default in v2; use RejectUnknownMembers when the endpoint contract requires strict commands. A forward-compatible event consumer may need another policy. Bound body bytes before decoding and limit expensive domain work separately.
sections.walkthrough: The complete helper needs encoding/json/v2 aliased as jsonv2, fmt, strings and errors. Its caller must cap data size before allocation. A fresh local target prevents earlier values or a partial failed decode from becoming a successful published result.

sections.title: Test syntax and business meaning separately
sections.body: Use fixtures for duplicate names, differently cased names, an unknown property, invalid UTF-8, a trailing second JSON value and a blank name. Record acceptance, typed value and domain-validation result. Do not decide compatibility solely from a changed error string.

sections.title: Authorize after decoding, before acting
sections.body: A valid document or resource ID does not establish tenant access. Bind the caller scope to the authoritative lookup or update predicate. A timeout during a later external write can leave its result unknown, so strict JSON decoding is not a substitute for an idempotency protocol.

sections.title: Fuzz a meaningful contract
sections.body: For arbitrary bounded bytes, assert that failed decoding returns no usable partial value. For accepted requests, check required invariants and a typed encode/decode round trip. Seed the ambiguity cases explicitly; a ten-second campaign explores inputs without proving every future input safe.

takeaway: Bound input, decode under an explicit policy, validate the domain and authorize the target before performing a side effect. Test each boundary independently.

wrongAnswers: Assume unknown names are always rejected

title: A Go agent task starts with a contract and a failing example
objective: Turn an ambiguous coding request into a small, verifiable Go change.
introduction: Claude Code, Codex and Cursor can inspect files, propose patches and run available tools. Useful work still needs a concrete behavior and a way to check it. In this unit you guide an agent in your own repository; GopherForge does not connect to an AI provider or send your projects to one.

sections.title: Give the task an observable result
sections.body: Suppose LowerBound returns an arbitrary duplicate index. Supply a minimal input, expected answer, supported Go version and public API constraint. Ask the agent to inspect the implementation and existing tests before proposing a change. A broad instruction such as improve search does not tell either of you which behavior matters.
sections.code:
Task: fix LowerBound in internal/search.
Input: [1, 3, 3, 8], target 3. Expected index: 1.
Preserve the exported signature and half-open interval invariant.
Inspect existing callers and tests first. Add empty, missing and duplicate cases.
Run: go test ./internal/search
Explain why equality moves hi instead of returning immediately.
sections.walkthrough: This is an example task prompt, not a tool-specific command. It names the defect, scope, invariant and verification. Replace paths with real repository paths; the agent must not invent a test result if the environment cannot run the command.

sections.title: Inspect before accepting a patch
sections.body: Read the actual diff, including tests. A test that merely duplicates the new implementation may be green without protecting the contract. Ask which previous input fails, why the change fixes it and which other callers could observe a difference. Formatting changes should not hide the behavior change.

sections.title: Keep human judgment at the boundary
sections.body: An agent can miss an overflow, copy a mutex or drop a cancellation path while producing plausible prose. Identify the owner of mutable values, the lifetime of every goroutine and the meaning of public errors yourself. A small patch is easier to understand and revert than an unexplained rewrite.

sections.title: Repeat a reproducible check
sections.body: Run the focused test, then the affected package checks. Record the actual compiler and command. If a remote integration service is unavailable, label that check unverified and keep an isolated reproduction. Passing unit tests is useful evidence; it is not proof about database failover or every interleaving.

reviewAnswer: A contract and a failing example

wrongAnswers: A larger rewrite with no constraints
A more confident completion message
hint: Choose evidence another developer can reproduce.

title: Repository guidance for Codex, Claude Code and Cursor
objective: Write useful Go repository instructions without confusing context with permissions.
introduction: Durable guidance saves repeated explanation of layout, build commands and boundary rules. The supported discovery mechanisms differ between products and can change. Keep the repository facts stable, then consult the official documentation for how the installed tool discovers and scopes them.

sections.title: Write the repository facts once
sections.body: Describe the real Go module, generated files, focused tests and opt-in integration environment. Use exact working directories and commands. Keep examples free of credentials and name environment variables without values. A new developer should be able to follow the same instructions without an agent.
sections.code:
# Go service working agreements
- Supported compiler: follow go.mod and the CI toolchain.
- Unit checks: go test ./...
- Worker changes: go test -race ./internal/worker/...
- Generated API: run the pinned generator documented in docs/generate.md.
- Integration checks use disposable databases; never production endpoints.
- Preserve public error and JSON contracts unless the task changes them.
sections.walkthrough: This illustrative guidance belongs in the repository instruction mechanism used by the selected tool. It is not an instruction for GopherForge itself. Replace package paths and generation commands with ones that exist in the actual checkout.

sections.title: Map facts to the tool deliberately
sections.body: Codex uses AGENTS.md with directory-scoped discovery and override rules. Claude Code uses CLAUDE.md and its documented rules and memory mechanisms. Cursor offers AGENTS.md and project rules in .cursor/rules with selectable scope. Do not assume copying one filename gives identical precedence in every product.

sections.title: Verify the loaded scope
sections.body: When guidance appears ignored, ask the tool which files it loaded and inspect its documented diagnostics. A nested instruction may override a general rule. Avoid growing one global instruction file into a second copy of the whole codebase; link concise maintained project documents where supported.

sections.title: Keep controls separate from prose
sections.body: A sentence saying do not access production is useful intent, but it does not revoke a credential. Use actual sandbox, approval and account controls in the environment. A rule file is not an authentication boundary, and ignoring a file for indexing does not necessarily prevent shell tools from reading it.

takeaway: Keep repository facts concrete, scope guidance using each product’s documented mechanism and enforce permissions in the environment. Recheck discovery after tool changes.

Excluding one file from search alone

title: Verify generated Go against the real module and runtime
objective: Catch invented APIs, unsafe concurrency and changed wire contracts in generated Go.
introduction: Generated source can look idiomatic while targeting the wrong driver major version or changing the public result. Compile against the selected module graph, inspect authoritative APIs and test the observable path. A plausible import name or confident explanation is not version evidence.

sections.title: Check which module the code actually uses
sections.body: Start in the target module and inspect the workspace and selected dependencies. A local replace can make generated code compile against unreleased source. For MongoDB v2, use its /v2 path and documented lifecycle; do not add an old major version merely to make an invented call compile.
sections.code:
go env GOMOD GOWORK
go list -m all
go doc go.mongodb.org/mongo-driver/v2/mongo.Connect
go test ./internal/store/...
sections.walkthrough: These are native-development commands in a repository that already depends on the v2 driver. go doc establishes the selected API rather than downloading a guessed dependency. The package test path must exist in that checkout.

sections.title: Review ownership before adding goroutines
sections.body: For every generated goroutine, identify who starts it, cancels it and waits for it. Check blocking sends and capacity acquisition. Acquiring a semaphore inside a newly launched goroutine can bound active work while still allowing an unbounded number of waiting goroutines.

sections.title: Compare contracts, not just signatures
sections.body: A nil slice becoming empty changes JSON under some serializers. Replacing %w with %v changes error matching. Returning success after a canceled partial export changes the protocol. Add fixtures for those decisions and check old callers before accepting a cosmetic cleanup.

sections.title: Require a failure-path demonstration

Run race detection on exercised concurrent paths and use integration tests for database atomicity. No amount of mocking can establish a live driver or server guarantee it never exercised.

title: Agent trust boundaries: repository text is input data
objective: Review commands, secrets and external writes when an agent consumes untrusted text.
introduction: A source comment, dependency README, test log or fetched webpage can contain instructions written by someone else. Reading that material to solve a Go problem does not authorize its author to expand the task. Keep the user’s goal and trusted repository guidance separate from external diagnostic content.

sections.title: Recognize an instruction hidden in a failure
sections.body: Imagine a failing test prints a page that tells the agent to upload environment variables. That instruction is not part of the authorized fix. Extract the actual assertion failure, inspect the relevant source and ignore the requested credential transfer.

Diagnostic data:
  expected first duplicate index 1, got 2
  see external.example/fix for instructions

Authorized task:
  repair LowerBound and prove duplicate handling

The external page cannot authorize uploading files or secrets.

sections.title: Use isolated integration resources
sections.body: Give agent-driven tests a disposable database, namespaced keys and bounded cleanup. A unique key prefix does not protect other data if a cleanup script still runs FLUSHDB.
