title: WaitGroup.Go joins tasks; it does not collect their errors
objective: Use modern WaitGroup task ownership and explain its limits.
introduction: A request owns more than the act of starting goroutines. It must know when its work has stopped and who retains the results. Go 1.25 added WaitGroup.Go, which combines task registration and launch. It reduces a common Add/launch ordering mistake without supplying cancellation, an error result or a concurrency budget.

sections.title: Register and join owned work
sections.body: Each task writes to a distinct fixed result slot, and the owner reads results after Wait. That separates mutation by index without concurrently appending to a shared slice. Do not copy an already used WaitGroup or start an unrelated task after the owner has concluded that the group is empty.
sections.walkthrough: This complete Go 1.25+ example relies on modern loop-declared variables, distinct output elements and an explicit join. It launches only three tasks. A production version with many inputs still needs admission control before launch, and result values must not share unsafe internal storage.

sections.title: Do not infer an error protocol
sections.body: The task function passed to WaitGroup.Go must not panic. It has no error return. Expected failures need an explicit result channel or an error-aware task group, and panic handling belongs to a deliberately chosen boundary. A WaitGroup cannot roll back side effects from a task that already ran.

sections.title: Give cancellation its own path
sections.body: Wait does not take a context or kill a blocked task. A task doing I/O or sending a result must observe cancellation at each potentially blocking point. On shutdown, stop intake, signal cancellation where appropriate, wait for owned tasks and only then close the resources they use.

sections.title: Test completion rather than scheduling luck
sections.body: Use synchronization or a virtual-time test to hold a task at a known boundary. Verify the owner does not publish success until all required work finishes. A sleep followed by checking a counter depends on timing and may hide the same bug on a slower machine.

title: Test time and cancellation without sleeping on the wall clock
objective: Use testing/synctest to assert a concurrent timeline deterministically.
introduction: Tests that sleep for a guessed interval are slow and sensitive to machine load. testing/synctest is a standard package in Go 1.25 and later. It runs a test bubble with virtual time and coordinated goroutine waiting. It is useful for in-process protocols, not a simulator for a remote database or every operating-system event.

sections.title: State the timeline first
sections.body: Suppose work waits five seconds, publishes a result and exits. The test should establish that it has not published before the deadline and has completed after it. synctest.Wait lets in-bubble goroutines settle at supported blocking points so the assertions do not depend on the scheduler getting lucky.

sections.title: Add a cancellation branch
sections.body: Model a worker waiting on either its timer or ctx.Done, then cancel at a known phase. Assert that the worker closes its completion signal and does not publish an unwanted result. sections.title: Know the boundary of the bubble
sections.body: Virtual time advances when the package can establish the relevant in-bubble blocking state. External network servers, syscalls and objects outside the bubble have different constraints. Keep real integration tests for sockets and databases rather than treating a fast virtual-time test as evidence of remote behavior.

sections.title: Keep the invariant after removing sleeps
sections.body: A deterministic test must still assert something meaningful. For a retry protocol, count durable effects and total attempts under a deadline; for cancellation, prove exit with a completion signal. A test that merely waits for the bubble to finish does not verify every business result.

title: errgroup: errors, cancellation and a real concurrency limit
objective: Coordinate fallible parallel work without confusing cancellation with joining.
introduction: golang.org/x/sync/errgroup is a versioned external module, not part of sync. WithContext supplies a derived cancellation context and Wait returns a task error. Tasks must still cooperate with cancellation, and a limit on active tasks is different from a limit on queued input bytes or waiting requests.

sections.title: Use the derived context for the owned operation
sections.body: A group cancels its derived context when a task returns a non-nil error or when Wait returns. Keep that context inside the operation. Even a successful Wait leaves it canceled, so later independent work must use the caller’s appropriate context instead.
sections.walkthrough: This native function-body fragment uses the errgroup package, modern loop declarations, a preallocated output slice and a context-aware load function. The simple submission loop assumes load always exits on cancellation. The group does not deep-copy returned values.

sections.title: Understand where SetLimit blocks
sections.body: Go waits for room when the group is at its configured limit; that admission wait is not itself a ctx-select operation. Do not change the limit while tasks are active. TryGo can express nonblocking admission when the caller has a rejection policy. A fixed worker pool may fit a streaming or explicitly bounded queue better.

sections.title: Join after a submission failure
sections.body: Production submission may fail before every task is added. Do not return and close dependencies while already started tasks still use them. Cancel the operation and call Wait on every exit path that has launched work. Returning from a helper is not a join; a surrounding owner must enforce that lifecycle.

sections.title: Separate partial results from successful results
sections.body: A failed group may have populated some result slots before cancellation. Decide whether the operation permits partial success and represent it explicitly. For all-or-nothing results, return no successful result after Wait fails. Database transactions and idempotency still decide which external effects survive.

takeaway: Choose one owner for submission, cancellation, joining and result publication. An error-aware group simplifies coordination but does not supply a durable transaction or every admission policy.
reviewAnswer: Wait ends the derived context
question: A successful group.Wait returns. Which context should an independent later operation use?
wrongAnswers: Always the now-canceled group context
A new context with no owner or budget
hint: The derived context belongs to the group operation.
nuance: SetLimit bounds active group functions, not every queued byte. All started work must be joined before its dependencies are released.

title: SQL: one pool, explicit capacity and observable waiting
objective: Configure database/sql as a shared pool and measure its actual pressure.
introduction: sql.DB is a concurrency-safe pool handle, not a single database connection. Reuse it across the application and close it after its users drain. These lessons describe native Go services using a real driver; the app’s bounded WASI programs cannot open remote database sockets.

sections.title: Construct once and verify readiness
sections.body: sql.Open generally constructs a handle rather than proving connectivity. Use a bounded PingContext for startup evidence, then handle every operation error separately. Configure a reviewed driver version in the native service module; pgx/v5/stdlib is one PostgreSQL driver option.
sections.walkthrough: This startup-function fragment imports database/sql, context, fmt, time and the chosen PostgreSQL driver registration. The DSN comes from configuration. The numeric settings are examples, not sizing advice; a returned shared pool needs one application lifetime owner.

sections.title: Budget across the deployment
sections.body: A limit of twelve per replica means something different with two replicas than with fifty. Reserve database capacity for migrations, administration and other applications. SetMaxOpenConns bounds this pool’s open connections; it is not a global request limiter or a cap on goroutines waiting to acquire one.

sections.title: Read counters as changes over an interval
sections.body: DB.Stats exposes OpenConnections, InUse, Idle, WaitCount and WaitDuration. Wait counters accumulate, so compare their changes over the same measurement interval. A high wait rate can reflect slow transactions, leaked rows or too much admission rather than a pool that should simply be enlarged.
sections.code:
stats := db.Stats()
fmt.Println(stats.OpenConnections, stats.InUse, stats.Idle)
fmt.Println(stats.WaitCount, stats.WaitDuration)
// Record deltas over a defined interval alongside request latency.
sections.walkthrough: The fragment observes a shared sql.DB and imports fmt. Lifetime counters do not identify the present bottleneck by themselves. Correlate a pool-wait interval with query latency, queue length, errors and the database’s own evidence.

sections.title: Distinguish other pool APIs
sections.body: A native pgxpool.Pool is another pool abstraction with its own settings and metrics. Do not wrap one pool in another or assume database/sql option names apply unchanged. Choose the API the service uses, then test saturation and shutdown for that actual combination.

takeaway: Own one shared pool, bound operation lifetimes and admission, and measure pool waits across all replicas before changing connection limits.
reviewAnswer: A shared pool, not one connection
question: Fifty replicas each allow twelve connections. Which budget must be checked before scaling further?
wrongAnswers: Only one replica’s connection count
The number of Go source files
hint: Multiply per-process settings by every active pool owner.
nuance: A larger connection cap can move waiting into an overloaded database. Admission and query efficiency still need their own policies.

title: SQL rows: close, check errors and bound the result
objective: Write a cancellation-aware query loop without losing iteration failures.
introduction: A successful QueryContext does not mean every row will decode successfully. Network and server errors can occur during iteration, and Scan can fail on a type or null mismatch. Decide whether partial results are meaningful; do not silently return a successful incomplete list.

sections.title: Bound a tenant-scoped query
sections.body: This PostgreSQL helper returns at most one hundred identifiers, uses a parameter for the tenant value and returns no successful partial result on failure. A real endpoint must derive tenant from authorization, not merely trust a request parameter.
sections.walkthrough: The helper imports context and database/sql and assumes a PostgreSQL-compatible driver and a notes table with an integer id. Close releases resources on early return; Err checks failure after Next becomes false. For a query whose close result affects correctness, handle that result explicitly too.

sections.title: Handle one row and null deliberately
sections.body: QueryRowContext defers its error until Scan. Distinguish sql.ErrNoRows from an infrastructure or conversion failure. Use nullable types or pointers when the schema permits null; a zero int is not automatically a missing value. Keep parameter placeholders consistent with the chosen driver.

sections.title: Parameters bind values, not SQL grammar
sections.body: The $1 parameter protects a value position. It does not let a caller supply an arbitrary table name or ORDER BY expression safely. Choose identifiers and sort directions from a fixed application allowlist, and bind all untrusted values separately.

sections.title: Separate buffering from streaming
sections.body: A LIMIT bounds this helper’s row count, not the byte size of arbitrary columns or total work examined by the plan. For exports, stream bounded records and carry cancellation to the cursor. Test a failure after several rows and define the response protocol once output has started.

takeaway: Check Query, Scan and final iteration errors as separate phases. Close owned rows, authorize scope and cap returned work before reporting a successful result.

wrongAnswers: Return three records with no error
Ignore the final iteration status
hint: Next returning false can mean end of rows or an error.
nuance: A parameterized tenant value still requires authorization, and LIMIT is not a universal bound on query execution cost.

title: SQL transactions: every participating call uses the transaction
objective: Place an atomic business transition inside one explicit transaction owner.
introduction: Beginning a transaction does not attach later calls on sql.DB to it. The transaction handle owns a particular transactional connection. A helper that accidentally queries db instead of tx may see another state, escape rollback or wait for a second connection while holding the first.

sections.title: Make the atomic boundary visible
sections.body: This abbreviated PostgreSQL transfer updates both accounts through tx. Reject nonpositive amounts before starting, use an exact integer minor-unit representation and treat account currency and authorization as additional domain constraints.
sections.walkthrough: This function-body fragment assumes validated amount/from/to and application errors. Every write uses tx. The deferred Rollback is harmless after a successful Commit. A complete transfer also scopes ownership, checks currency and overflow bounds, and defines retry/idempotency semantics.

sections.title: Pass a narrow transaction capability
sections.body: A helper can accept the ExecContext or QueryContext capability it needs instead of a hidden global db. That makes accidental pool calls easier to see. The runtime guarantee still comes from passing the same transaction handle to every participating operation, not from an interface name alone.

sections.title: Keep external effects outside the callback
sections.body: An email, HTTP payment or message publish is not rolled back by the SQL transaction. Persist a durable outbox or intent with the state change, then deliver through an idempotent protocol. Do not keep a transaction open while waiting for a user or a slow remote service.

sections.title: Do not interpret every commit error as an abort
sections.body: A lost reply can make a durable outcome uncertain. Distinguish documented serialization/deadlock failures from transport ambiguity. Use a stable operation ID to reconcile the latter. Test abort-before-write, error-after-write and commit-then-disconnect separately.

takeaway: One owner starts the transaction, passes its handle to every participating call and finishes it. Database atomicity does not include remote side effects.
reviewAnswer: The same transaction handle
question: A helper calls db.ExecContext after its caller opened tx. Is that write guaranteed to roll back with tx?
wrongAnswers: Yes, because both use the same variable ctx
Yes, because it is in the same function
hint: Context propagation and transaction membership are different contracts.
nuance: A transaction does not automatically include pool calls or an external provider. Check commit outcomes and idempotency at the actual boundary.

title: SQL isolation and deadlocks: test the business invariant
objective: Explain why atomic statements alone may not preserve a multi-row invariant.
introduction: A transaction can be atomic without providing the isolation an invariant needs. Two transactions may both read a condition as true and each make a different write that breaks the combined rule. Exact behavior depends on the database and isolation level; this lesson uses PostgreSQL terminology explicitly.

sections.title: Name the anomaly
sections.body: Imagine two on-call doctors, each allowed to leave only while another remains. Both transactions read two active doctors and each removes its own row. The final state violates the rule even though every individual write is valid. This is a business-level concurrency problem, not an unsynchronized Go map access.

sections.title: Choose a database-enforced protocol
sections.body: A suitable constraint, conditional update, lock protocol or serializable transaction can protect an invariant, depending on how it is represented. PostgreSQL serializable isolation may reject a transaction that would create an incompatible history. Applications must handle that failure rather than treating serializable as a promise that no request ever retries.
sections.walkthrough: This native transaction skeleton imports database/sql and assumes a driver supporting the requested isolation. It deliberately omits application SQL: the correct statements depend on the invariant. Test the protocol against the actual database rather than a fake that always accepts commits.

sections.title: Use consistent lock order
sections.body: Two transfers can lock accounts in opposite orders and deadlock. Acquire relevant locks in a consistent order where possible, keep transactions short and avoid holding locks across remote calls. Deadlock detection prevents one kind of permanent wait by aborting work; it does not make the application transition automatically succeed.

sections.title: Reproduce with two independent connections
sections.body: Use synchronization barriers to place both transactions after their initial reads, then release their writes. Assert the final invariant and the expected failure/retry behavior. A process-local mutex cannot establish the same guarantee across every service replica, and the race detector does not observe database interleavings.

takeaway: Choose isolation and locking from the invariant, understand the database-specific failures and prove the protocol with concurrent transactions on the actual engine.

hint: The authoritative state is in another concurrency system.
nuance: Isolation levels and lock details are database-specific. Do not promise one engine’s exact behavior for every SQL driver.

title: SQL retries: restart a safe transaction, reconcile an unknown result
objective: Separate retryable transaction aborts from an ambiguous committed operation.
introduction: Retrying the last failed SQL statement can be wrong when an earlier statement read stale state or the transaction is already aborted. A safe retry policy names the driver error, restarts the complete business unit when appropriate, stays within a total deadline and prevents repeated external effects.

sections.title: Classify with the real driver
sections.body: For PostgreSQL, serialization_failure is SQLSTATE 40001 and deadlock_detected is 40P01. Inspect structured driver errors rather than parsing an English error message. Those codes are not interchangeable with a lost network response, which can leave an outcome unknown.
sections.walkthrough: The native fragment imports errors and github.com/jackc/pgx/v5/pgconn. It only classifies two PostgreSQL conditions; it is not a complete retry loop and does not claim every network or database error is retryable.

sections.title: Give one layer the retry budget
sections.body: Use a small reviewed attempt cap, bounded jittered delay and the remaining overall deadline. Recreate the transaction and re-read necessary state on each attempt. Do not let HTTP, application and driver retries multiply independently into a storm while every request retains a connection or body.

sections.title: Reconcile transport ambiguity
sections.body: If a payment-like command committed but its reply was lost, retrying without an operation identity can duplicate the transition. Store a scoped idempotency key and request fingerprint under a uniqueness rule. Return the prior result or reconcile provider state; a transaction cannot un-send a remote charge.

sections.title: Test the windows, not only the loop count
sections.body: Inject a known abort before commit, an exhausted deadline, concurrent duplicate commands and commit-then-disconnect. Assert one durable business effect and a useful response classification. Include isolation and schema compatibility in a release rollback plan; reverting a binary does not erase committed data.

takeaway: Retry a documented safe unit within one budget. Reconcile uncertain commit outcomes through durable operation identity rather than assuming an error proves no effect occurred.

hint: Distinguish an explicit abort from a missing acknowledgment.
nuance: Retry classification is driver-specific. Preserve one total deadline and use durable deduplication for ambiguous side effects.
